title: 4 takeaways from the Ravens’ preseason win over the Vikings
summary: The Baltimore Ravens earned another solid preseason win over the Minnesota Vikings to continue a perfect start to the Jesse Minter era. Here are a few main takeaways from the victory. Even after Danny Pinter’s injury, the center competition is in good shape. While Jovaughn Gwyn wasn’t as good as last week, I think the […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - AUGUST 15: Ryan Eckley #30 of the Baltimore Ravens punts the ball against the Philadelphia Eagles during the first half of a preseason game at M&T Bank Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens earned another solid preseason win over the Minnesota Vikings to continue a perfect start to the Jesse Minter era. Here are a few main takeaways from the victory. Even after Danny Pinter’s injury, the center competition is in good shape. While Jovaughn Gwyn wasn’t as good as last week, I think the tape will show he wasn’t horrendous and the overall offensive line struggles were more a product of Brian Flores being absolutely mad in the head. Ethan Pocic had his first significant action and playing for two entire quarters, and while it was against second- and third-string talent, Pocic looked healthy, which is the priority right now. You aren’t worried about a veteran of his caliber facing better competition but rather how his body plays and responds coming off an Achilles injury. Either way, one of those guys will fill in and hopefully don’t drag the entire unit down to being bottom-five in the league. The death of the Ravens’ TE room was greatly exaggerated. The departures of Isaiah Likely and Charlie Kolar are big losses that shouldn’t be understated, but it seems the Ravens have quickly filled the void in the aggregate. Matt Hibner had a great performance last week, opening up the offense with a 29-yard wheel route and finishing with 61 yards on five catches. Josh Cuevas followed it up this week with 46 yards on three catches, including an acrobatic grab. Mark Andrews will do what he always has — find the soft spots in zone and be a safety blanket for Lamar Jackson, even if his explosive plays and yards after catch days are done. Durham Smythe will be a solid blocking tight end and fill in where needed. While the ceiling for this room might not be as high as last year, the fall off for this unit in a new wide receiver-heavy scheme won’t sink this team like some might have thought early in training camp. Ethan Burke should get the 5th OLB roster spot. Burke has constantly popped on film and looks to be a good player on special teams as well. This isn’t a knock against Adisa Isaac and Kaimon Rucker for being bad, but more an emphasis on Burke’s play. Isaac was in the right place at the right time against the Eagles to catch a bobbled ball and take it to the endzone for a pick-six. Unfortunately, it was called incomplete and he hasn’t been on the stat sheet otherwise. Rucker has a couple of tackles and a quarterback hit between the two games. But Burke has racked up five total tackles, a sack, a tackle for loss, two pass breakups, and two quarterback hits. He’s simply popped more and made more plays. Ryan Eckley could replace Jordan Stout as an elite punter right away. After shanking his first professional punt against the Eagles, Ryan Eckley done nothing but bomb punts down the field and pin teams deep. His second punt against the Eagles pinned them at the 10, and against the Vikings, Eckley totaled six punts that averaged 55.3 yards, with a long of 60 yards. Two of those six punts were inside the 20, with one landing at the 4-yard line. All jokes aside, it’s great to see Eckley bounce back from some and be a machine since. The Ravens were heavily favored by Jordan Stouts punting last season but Stouts first years in the league were average to below average. Not going back to that would be a huge boon for a team chasing a championship.

title: Discussion: overreactions to the Ravens’ preseason win over the Vikings
summary: The NFL preseason is ripe for overreactions, and today, Baltimore Beatdown wants to hear yours! The Ravens took home their second straight preseason victory under new head coach Jesse Minter on Saturday with a dominant defensive showing against the Vikings. The offense, especially the run game, had a quiet afternoon, but undrafted rookie quarterback Joe […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - AUGUST 15: Aeneas Peebles #90 of the Baltimore Ravens runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFL preseason football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at M&T Bank Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The NFL preseason is ripe for overreactions, and today, Baltimore Beatdown wants to hear yours! The Ravens took home their second straight preseason victory under new head coach Jesse Minter on Saturday with a dominant defensive showing against the Vikings. The offense, especially the run game, had a quiet afternoon, but undrafted rookie quarterback Joe Fagnano continued to impress with several strong throws with pressure in his face. Rookie punter Ryan Eckley took advantage of the busy day with 332 yards on six punts (55.3 yards per punt), including a 54-yard beauty that was fair-caught at Minnesota’s 4-yard line. Nikhil’s take: The Ravens’ defensive line will thrive with or without Nnamdi Madubuike. The Ravens have long been known for developing defensive line talent, but even they could not bridge the gap when the unit was decimated by injuries last year. A potential return from Nnamdi Madubuike has raised expectations for the group, but when examined closely, the roster could be considered thin behind Travis Jones and Calais Campbell. John Jenkins turned 37 years old this summer, and Broderick Washington’s production was declining before his season-ending injury last year. The rest of the room is made up of unproven Day 3 picks and UDFAs. But Saturday’s preseason game showed that Baltimore has plenty of depth along the interior of their defensive line. Every active Ravens defensive tackle except Aaron Graves was credited with at least one pressure ( via Pro Football Focus ), with Aeneas Peebles registering four. (Graves has been plenty active in training camp and still logged a 66.2 pass rush grade from PFF.) Rayshaun Benny and David Olajiga both recorded sacks; Olajiga in particular had a quick, clean pass rush win from a nose tackle alignment, darting around Vikings center Vershon Lee in a flash. Madubuike has been gradually ramping up throughout camp, but if he does not graduate to some form of contact this week, he will be unlikely to be ready for the start of the regular season. That would force the Ravens’ defensive line depth to play significant snaps early in the season with Washington and Jenkins probably seeing the most time. But depending on the opponent, Jesse Minter’s gameplan could call for an interior pass rush specialist like Peebles, a hulking presence like CJ Okoye, or any of the team’s other young defensive tackles. If Saturday was any indication, they’ll be ready. Now, it’s your turn! What’s your overreaction from the Ravens’ preseason win over the Vikings?

Among the potential targets: New England Patriots wide receiver Kayshon Boutte and Baltimore Ravens wide receiver Rashod Bateman. The potential for Bateman to be suspended for violating the NFL’s personal conduct policy may have been a non-starter for the Texans, but the Ravens may not be interested in moving the 2021 first-round pick, either. Bateman is coming off career-low numbers virtually across the board, but he has seemed revitalized in a more diverse role in Declan Doyle’s new offense, including plenty of time in the slot. He also remains on an affordable contract for a WR2. But if rookie receivers Ja’Kobi Lane and Elijah Sarratt both prove themselves this year, Bateman could be a trade piece next offseason. Kyle Hamilton makes The Athletic’s 25 under 25 Meet the NFL’s top players 25 and under. Coaches, scouts, execs rank them heading into 2026 – Mike Jones (The Athletic) Year 4 saw Hamilton top the 100-tackle mark for the second straight season. The two-time first-team All-Pro selection boasts great range when playing deep safety and flexes his versatility even more when matching up with receivers in the slot. PFF offers biggest reasons for optimism, concern about Ravens Reasons for optimism for all 32 NFL teams – Gordon McGuinness (Pro Football Focus) Doyle learned under Sean Payton and Ben Johnson, so expect the Ravens to lean more on three-receiver sets and use plenty of motion. It’s also worth noting that while Jackson had a down year, he earned a 91.4 PFF overall grade over his final four games of the season. That came just one year after he earned a 94.0 PFF overall grade and posted a 41-to-4 touchdown-to-interception ratio. Jesse Minter replacing John Harbaugh doesn’t just give the Ravens a fresh perspective at the top; it should also boost a defense that has struggled in recent years — Minter ran a Chargers defense that ranked inside the NFL’s top 10 in expected points added (EPA) allowed on defense in each of the past two seasons. Hendrickson should also provide a significant boost to the pass rush. He has earned a PFF pass-rush grade above 90.0 in each of the past three seasons, something no Ravens edge defender has accomplished since Elvis Dumervil in 2013. Biggest concern for every NFL team entering the 2026 season – Gordon McGuinness (Pro Football Focus) The interior of the offensive line is still a question mark. On one hand, Vega Ioane and John Simpson should be upgrades over Daniel Faalele and Andrew Vorhees, but Ioane’s lack of NFL experience means the Ravens may have to accept some growing pains. They also lost center Tyler Linderbaum to the Raiders in free agency. While the addition of Pocic helps, he is still a step down from a player who ranked fifth among all centers in PFF overall grade last season.

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: defensive lineman Deone Walker
summary: With the Buffalo Bills introducing a new defensive scheme this season, there have come questions about how the players on the roster fit new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s vision. After former head coach and defensive designer Sean McDermott was fired, the team has seemed to embrace a more physical, aggressive approach in their defensive preparations. […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 15: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers gets sacked by Deone Walker #96 of the Buffalo Bills during the first half at Highmark Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images With the Buffalo Bills introducing a new defensive scheme this season, there have come questions about how the players on the roster fit new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s vision. After former head coach and defensive designer Sean McDermott was fired, the team has seemed to embrace a more physical, aggressive approach in their defensive preparations. Rather than relying on sound adherence to place and assignment, the Bills are prioritizing playing quickly as the assignment. One of the positions on the roster that has garnered plenty of discussion is that of the nose tackle. In a 3-down front like Leonhard has implemented, that position is essential to the rest of the defensive line’s success. Truthfully, this isn’t too different from how McDermott’s scheme operated, as the “one-tech” position was analogous to the nost tackle in that it was the spot that allowed the other players on defense to shine. Without a strong player in the middle, the defense is set to struggle. Do the Bills already have that strong player at the nose? In today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we’ll discuss the team’s presumed nose tackle. Spoiler alert: He’s a stud. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Deone Walker Number: 96 Position: DL Height/Weight: 6’7” 331 lbs. Age: 22 (23 on 3/11/2027) Experience/Draft: 2; selected by Buffalo in the fourth round (No. 109 overall) of the 2025 NFL Draft College: Kentucky Acquired: Fourth-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Walker enters the second year of his four-year rookie contract, which is worth $5,247,040 overall. In 2026, Walker carries a cap hit of $1,266,760 if he makes the 53-man roster. If he’s released, the Bills will carry a dead cap charge of $785,280. 2025 Recap: After a collegiate season where a back injury limited Walker’s explosiveness, he slid all the way to the fourth round in the 2025 NFL Draft. The Bills scooped him up, and they have reaped the benefits since. Walker was excellent as a rookie, playing in all 17 games and serving as a point of consistency in the middle of a defense wrecked by injuries. Walker totaled 39 tackles, eight tackles for loss, four pass knockdowns, four quarterback hits, one fumble recovery, and one sack during the regular season. He played 464 defensive snaps, good for 47% of the team’s total on defense, as veteran Ed Oliver missed nearly the whole season thanks to a litany of injuries. That snap total was the highest among Bills’ defensive tackles, as veteran DaQuan Jones also missed five games. In the playoffs, Walker was still a wrecking ball, and he put together two very good games. He had six tackles, two pass knockdowns, and an interception while generally wreaking havoc on both the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Denver Broncos. Positional outlook: Walker is set to start at the nose, with DeWayne Carter, Phidarian Mathis (who is suspended for the first three regular season games due to a violation of the NFL’s substance abuse policy), and Zion Logue also playing snaps at that spot. The other defensive linemen on the roster are Tommy Akingbesote, Ed Oliver, Zane Durant, Landon Jackson, Travis Clayton, and T.J. Sanders. 2026 Offseason: Walker is healthy and he has played well this summer. He was only on the field for ten snaps in Buffalo’s preseason opener against the Carolina Panthers, but he was a menace. Walker had a sack, three tackles, two QB pressures, and one tackle for loss. 2026 Season outlook: Buffalo Bills general manager Brandon Beane has done a good job in the middle rounds of his drafts, and it seems like he’s found another mid-round gem in Walker. The big fella is versatile enough where he really could play any role along Jim Leonhard’s three-man front and he’ll find success. That leads to the question of whether the team wants him to be the nose tackle long-term, or do they think it would serve him—and the team—best to play more as a penetrating attacker. If the Bills were looking at Walker as a traditional nose tackle—think Ted Washington—then Walker will be successful. However, he was at his best last season when he was replacing Oliver as the penetrating three-tech player. An overly simple explanation of the difference in roles comes down to gap responsibilities. A one-tech (or zero-tech, as a nose would be considered) is often expected to control more than one blocker as part of his responsibility. As players go farther away from the middle, many defenses ask those linemen to exploit one-on-one matchups, and those matchups are often exploitable because of the success of the big fella in the middle. Leonhard’s defense seems to be less concerned about the gap assignments and more concerned with causing chaos in opposing backfields. That should give Walker (and the rest of Buffalo’s defensive line) plenty of freedom to make plays. That freedom was on full display during Buffalo’s preseason opener, and while any exhibition results should be digested with caution, there were plenty of reasons to be optimistic. Walker, both literally and figuratively, was one of the biggest reasons for optimism. So long as Walker stays healthy, he’s going to have a huge role on the Bills’ defense this season. If his early play is any indication, he might become a household name sooner rather than later.

title: Projecting Buffalo Bills 2026 practice squad before Steelers preseason game
summary: The Buffalo Bills will have to make roster cutdown decisions after their third preseason game against the Pittsburgh Steelers inside the new Highmark Stadium on Thursday night. Fortunately for the Bills, they’ll technically have plenty of time to mull over those decisions, as this year’s roster cutdown deadline isn’t until Sunday, August 30 at 6:00pm […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - AUGUST 22: Wide receiver Ja'mori MacLin #84 of the Buffalo Bills catches a pass over cornerback Tre Avery #11 of the Cleveland Browns during the second quarter of the preseason game at Huntington Bank Field on August 22, 2026, in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills will have to make roster cutdown decisions after their third preseason game against the Pittsburgh Steelers inside the new Highmark Stadium on Thursday night. Fortunately for the Bills, they’ll technically have plenty of time to mull over those decisions, as this year’s roster cutdown deadline isn’t until Sunday, August 30 at 6:00pm EST. Before the Bills final preseason game of 2026 takes place, let’s attempt to project the club’s practice squad for this season. Practice squads have been low-key important elements to a team’s roster throughout every season. I’ll update my projection — if applicable — after the exhibition outing against the Steelers. But first, some practice squad rules: After COVID, NFL practice squads were cemented at 16 players. Up to six veterans are allowed. They can have an unlimited number of accrued seasons in the NFL. The remaining 10 spots must be reserved for players with two or fewer accrued professional seasons. One extra spot is available — to make a club’s practice squad 17 players — for the International Pathway Program. *A player needs to be on the 53-man roster for a total of six or more regular season games to earn an accrued season. For reference, at the outset of the 2025 regular season, this is what the Bills practice squad looked like: WR: Kristian Wilkerson, Stephen Gosnell OT: Travis Clayton (IPP) OG: Kendrick Green OC: Dan Feeney TE: Keleki Latu QB: Shane Buechele RB: Frank Gore Jr. EDGE: Andre Jones Jr. DL: Jordan Phillips, Zion Logue LB: Keonta Jenkins, Jimmy Ciarlo CB: Dane Jackson, Jalen Kimber S: Jordan Poyer, Sam Franklin Now onto 2026 — who currently on Bills roster would qualify for the 10-spot young-player stipulation in the NFL’s practice squad rules, you ask? They’re listed below: ( I’ve purposely left off those youngsters who aren’t in real jeopardy of being cut and subject to practice-squad consideration ) WR: Ja’Mori Maclin, Max Tomczak, Mac Dalena, Stephen Gosnell, Quentin Skinner OL: Chase Lundt, Da’Metrius Weatherspoon, Ar’maj Reed-Adams, Bruno Fina TE: Keleki Latu RB: Ian Wheeler, Frank Gore Jr. QB: Shane Buechele OLB: Cade Denhoff, Andre Jones Jr. DL: Zion Logue, Zane Durant LB: Keonta Jenkins, Theron Gaines, Jimmy Ciarlo CB: Kani Walker, Toriano Pride Jr., Jordan Dunbar S: Te’Cory Couch, Wande Owens And now here’s my practice squad projection ahead of Buffalo’s final 2026 preseason game against the Pittsburgh Steelers. I have bolded names of the veteran members. My Buffalo Bills 2026 practice squad projection WR: Ja’Mori Maclin, Stephen Gosnell OL: Chase Lundt, Ar’maj Reed-Adams TE: Keleki Latu, Shane Zylstra RB: Frank Gore Jr. QB: Shane Buechele OLB: Andre Jones Jr. DL: Zion Logue LB: Joe Andreessen, Jimmy Ciarlo CB: Toriano Pride Jr., Jordan Dunbar S: Te’Cory Couch, Wande Owens IPP: DT Travis Clayton Only going with three veterans gives the Bills plenty of space to add veterans later if need be. At receiver, Maclin’s spot on the practice squad feels distinctly secure right now, and I think the Bills like the developmental upside of Gosnell, who has three catches for 44 yards in two preseason games. Latu and Zylstra probably have the best chances to see the field during the regular season. In short, if the numbers game wasn’t a thing, I believe they’d both be on Buffalo’s roster. Gore Jr. and Ian Wheeler, the latter of whom I have on Buffalo’s 53-man roster in my latest projection , are interchangeable. I could see the Bills opting with either of them to start the regular season on the regular roster. Lundt is the long-term developmental offensive tackle. Reed-Adams is that player on the inside, and I like his potential more. Logue is a classic 4i/5tech project, and Durant is the long-term option to play 0T, 1T or even some 3T in time. Andreessen and Ciarlo have shown well enough this summer — particularly in the preseason — to be valuable practice squad members. The defensive backs — Pride Jr., Dunbar, Owens, and Couch — are kept on versatility alone. They can align anywhere due to their suddenness and experience wearing many hats. What do you think? Would you make any chances to this practice squad ahead of Buffalo’s last preseason game of the summer?

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: safety Cole Bishop
summary: The Buffalo Bills are looking to forge a new defensive identity in the post-Sean McDermott era. While McDermott’s defenses were known to include multiple checks and relied on the ability of its players to know their individual assignments—doing their “one-eleventh”—the Bills’ defense in 2026 is looking to be more physical and more aggressive than its […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - JANUARY 11: Cole Bishop #24 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates with teammates after intercepting a pass during the fourth quarter against the Jacksonville Jaguars in the AFC Wild Card Playoff game at EverBank Stadium on January 11, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Megan Briggs/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills are looking to forge a new defensive identity in the post-Sean McDermott era. While McDermott’s defenses were known to include multiple checks and relied on the ability of its players to know their individual assignments—doing their “one-eleventh”—the Bills’ defense in 2026 is looking to be more physical and more aggressive than its previous iterations. In today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss a young safety whose best football is ahead of him, and whose overall style of play is likely to benefit tremendously from the new scheme. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Cole Bishop Number: 24 Position: S Height/Weight: 6’2” 206 lbs. Age: 23 (24 on 10/24/2026) Experience/Draft: 3; selected by Buffalo in the second round (No. 60 overall) of the 2024 NFL Draft College: Utah Acquired: Second-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Bishop enters the third year of his rookie contract, a four-year pact worth $6,547,996 overall. For the 2026 season, Bishop’s cap hit is $1,785,817 if he makes the 53-man roster. Buffalo will carry a dead cap hit of $791,090 if he’s released. 2025 Recap: After an up-and-down rookie season that saw Bishop experience plenty of growing pains in limited field time, he showed the tremendous potential Buffalo saw when they drafted him in Round Two of the 2024 NFL Draft. He started all 19 of Buffalo’s games, including both playoff contests, and led the team in total tackles on the season with 85. He made his first career interception on a circus catch to stop a potential touchdown drive in Buffalo’s 31-19 victory over the New Orleans Saints in Week Four. His second and third career interceptions came in consecutive weeks, as he intercepted Tua Tagovailoa in Buffalo’s 30-13 loss at Miami in Week Ten and Bake Mayfield in Buffalo’s 44-32 victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week Eleven. He also clinched Buffalo’s 27-24 Wild Card victory over the Jacksonville Jaguars with another acrobatic interception on Trevor Lawrence’s final attempt of the game. Against Bo Nix and the Denver Broncos, he allowed all six passes thrown his way to be completed for a ttoal of 80 yards, but he also led the team in tackles in the game with 12. He totaled 85 tackles, seven pass breakups, three interceptions, two sacks, and four tackles for loss in the regular season. Positional outlook: Bishop is one of six players listed at safety on the current roster. Jalen Kilgore, C.J. Gardner-Johnson, Damar Hamlin, Geno Stone, and Wande Owens are the others. Sam Franklin is listed at defensive back, but he is a safety when he’s not playing on special teams. Jordan Hancock is also listed at defensive back, and he plays a hybrid role as a slot corner and safety. 2026 Offseason: Bishop missed time this summer due to a shoulder issue; he sat out the team’s preseason opener as a result of the injury. However, he has since returned to practice. He also had a minor knee scope in the offseason. 2026 Season outlook: There are some uncertainties about Buffalo’s new-look defense in terms of role, but Bishop is a clear starter at safety. He is likely to start alongside Gardner-Johnson when both players are healthy, and while both of them have missed time this summer due to injury, it seems that their absence has been mostly precautionary. Bishop is a phenomenal athlete who can help the defense in multiple phases and at multiple levels. He has the speed to patrol the back end of the defense, the toughness to mix it up in the run game, and the quickness and agility to handle everything in between. He has star potential from the safety position, and I think that he only scratched the surface of that potential last season. In new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s scheme, Bishop will likely be asked to do less reacting and more attacking, something that should help him to accentuate his athleticism. The principles he learned over the last two years in former head coach Sean McDermott’s scheme can easily be applied to other styles of defense, and now Leonhard can allow him to play more aggressively since he understands the nuances of the position. How fortunate for Bishop, really, that his former head coach was a safety, and now his new defensive coordinator was also a safety. Bishop has greater physical tools, though, than either his former coach or his current coach ever had. Leonhard, for his part, was a scrappy safety whose heart and mind propelled him to greater heights than his physical talents alone could have. If Bishop can continue to learn that mental part of the game from his current coordinator, look out, because that very good 2025 season could be the start of something outstanding.

Against the Cleveland Browns, Sherfield did a heck of a job saying… Video Time pic.twitter.com/Ch8SNGLu9Y — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) August 24, 2026 Now this comes with the usual preseason disclaimer about the opponent not planning for the game, not playing against the best, yada yada yada. That said, some of the things in that little film would be present regardless of the quality of competition. Sherfield’s ability to stop and cut back, his physicality blocking, and his ability to adjust to the catch would all be there no matter who is on the other side of the ball. Kyle Allen chucked the ball around rather nicely in Preseason Week 2, and a large part of why that was possible is named “Trent Sherfield.” Will it be enough to make the roster on the 2026 iteration of the Buffalo Bills? I think he’s making a very solid case for himself. Despite being on the wrong side of 30, Sherfield is still plenty athletic based on his preseason performance. He adds veteran savvy finding soft spots in coverage, and lining up correctly for blocking on run downs. There’s one more week of preseason action, and I know I’ll be keeping an eye on his snap counts against the Pittsburgh Steelers. If the usual preseason trends hold true, the less he plays, the better his odds are on making the 53.

title: What Bills vs. Browns really tells us about Buffalo’s depth chart
summary: Last week, I wrote an article that I will follow up on today. The premise of this article is that “when and with whom” a player plays in the preseason is more indicative of their overall roster placement than their actual performance and should be monitored for predictive purposes. I will copy the into concept […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 15: Alec Anderson #70 of the Buffalo Bills on the sideline against the Carolina Panthers at Highmark Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last week, I wrote an article that I will follow up on today. The premise of this article is that “when and with whom” a player plays in the preseason is more indicative of their overall roster placement than their actual performance and should be monitored for predictive purposes. I will copy the into concept below: Team-released preseason depth charts are mostly nonsense. The teams wouldn’t release them if the league didn’t make them, and what they say is utilized more as PR and internal player motivation that it is anything else. If you really want to know in the preseason how a team views a player, you have to start with the WAWW Factor. When and with whom (WAWW) a player plays in the preseason is far more indicative of their stance on the roster than how a player plays. If a depth cornerback absolutely crushes in in the last quarter of the final preseason game alongside a bunch of players who won’t make the team, his fate is probably already sealed. The fact that he’s playing great is wonderful; the fact that he’s playing in the last quarter of the final preseason game in tandem with other players who likely won’t make the team means he also won’t likely make the team. So what can the WAWW Factor from the preseason game versus the Cleveland Browns tell us about where certain players are located on the Buffalo Bills depth chart, especially at roster battle positions? Kani Walker v Toriano Pride Jr. (outside CB4) Last week, we saw Kani Walker come into the game later than Toriano Pride, Jr. We also saw Pride, not Walker, play on special teams. This was a footnote more than a flag plant because Walker was coming off a week when he missed practice, and I said we’d have to keep an eye on it this week. We kept and eye on it, and it looks like a dead heat. Walker came into the game earlier than Pride, Jr. (on the first play from scrimmage on defense, to be exact). Both CB4 candidates played until about the six minute mark of the fourth quarter. And both played on special teams. From a WAWW Factor standpoint, it looks like a dead heat, which means predictive tie goes to the player who appears to have performed the best. If you made me do a 53-man roster projection right now, I’d put Kani Walker in the outside CB4 spot. Keon Coleman and Joshua Palmer (WR3) Null data set. Keon Coleman did not play due to injury, and Joshua Palmer didn’t play as the otherwise WR3 because the skill position “starters” all rested. Kaleb Elarms-Orr (KEO) and Dorian Williams (LB2) Last week, KEO was clearly treated as LB3, entering the game with the second unit and getting no overlap with incumbent ILB Dorian Williams. That was not the case this week. KEO played the first defensive scrimmage snaps of the game and also special teams. And the end of the first half, Dorian Williams was still playing on defense and Elarms-Orr had already turned in his helmet for the day. It is interesting to note that Williams did not play any special teams snaps, but this LB2 battle looks more like an actual battle this week than it did last. Alec Anderson and Austin Corbett (LG) Anderson may be pulling ahead in the race to be the only starter on the Buffalo Bills offensive line who’s not on a long-term contract. The carryover from the 2025 Bills team and the former jumbo lineman once again found himself on the field on the first offensive snap from scrimmage. He was also left the game in the first quarter, while Corbett played into the second. Sedrick Van-Pran Granger and Lloyd Cushenberry (backup center) The Bills weren’t behaving like it was a competition last week, and that didn’t change against the Browns. Sedrick Van-Pran Granger played almost the entire game, and Lloyd Cushenberry didn’t play a single snap despite being healthy. Pack this one up folks; we may see Cushenberry week one against the Houston Texans if starter Connor McGovern isn’t ready to go after a hamstring injury suffered a few weeks ago. Trent Sherfield, Mecole Hardman, and Stephen Gosnell (WR6) Sherfield entered the earliest out of the three (on offense), exited the earliest, and played teams as one would expect. Hardman was next up in the “from scrimmage enter/exit” category, then Gosnell. Combined with the plays Sherfield made in the passing game, I’m still inclined to believe it’s his roster spot, but I remain less clear on it than other positions. The caveat here is that if rookie Skyler Bell isn’t able to make it for week one of the regular season, the Bills may decide to only keep five wide receivers. They may also keep six and two of Sherfield/Hardman/Gosnell make it temporarily. Maxwell Hairston and Davison Igbinosun (CB2) Cornerback Maxwell Hairston returned to practice this week but the ostensibly-healthy 2025 first round pick didn’t play against Cleveland, while 2026 second rounder Davison Igbinosun started and played until the middle of the second quarter. Nothing we’ve seen thus far would indicate than a healthy Hairston will not be the man opposite starter Christian Benford against the Texans on the first defensive snap of the regular season. As I mentioned last week, the line matter more than the dot. We now have two preseason game data points and we’ll stay tuned for the final one after the Bills play the Pittsburgh Steelers on Thursday night. …and that’s the way the cookie crumbles. I’m Bruce Nolan with Buffalo Rumblings. You can find me on Twitter and Instagram @BruceExclusive and look for new episodes of “The Bruce Exclusive” every Thursday on the Rumblings Cast Network — see more in my LinkTree!

title: Princely Umanmielen is ready and needed to have a break out year
summary: The Carolina Panthers broke a near decade long playoff drought last season and seem poised to enter the 2026 season with both momentum and an improved roster. One of the biggest aspects of that roster improvement was the development of now second-year players Nic Scourton and Princely Umanmielen and the marquee free agency signing of […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 15: Princely Umanmielen #3 of the Carolina Panthers looks to sack Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills during the first half at Highmark Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers broke a near decade long playoff drought last season and seem poised to enter the 2026 season with both momentum and an improved roster. One of the biggest aspects of that roster improvement was the development of now second-year players Nic Scourton and Princely Umanmielen and the marquee free agency signing of Jaelan Phillips. Together they were going to form the core of the best pass rushing group this team has seen in years. No wonder, then, that fans were devastated when Scourton tore his ACL in training camp. Scourton was a breakout player as a rookie and was set to start this season. All of those hopes now rest on Umanmielen, who most had pegged as a rotational player with some promise. Fast forward a couple of weeks and that promise has been flashing as realized talent on the field. Through two preseason games, Umanmielen has constantly stood out as one of the better players on the Panthers defense. Panthers fans even voted him as the most impressive player they watched in the otherwise disappointing loss to the Buffalo Bills in the first week of the preseason. While he may not be putting together eye-popping stats, he has been frequently in position to or inches away from making big plays in the backfield. He isn’t Julius Peppers in year six in the NFL, he is a second year player who saw limited playing time as a rookie. Nearly there is a sign a of progress at this point in his career. If you don’t trust your own eyes then consider trusting Pro Football Focus and his own teammates. Umanmielen was the second highest graded Panthers defensive player last week against the Jacksonville Jaguars and has been described by Phillips as “the best pass rusher on [the] team.” Carolina would obviously be better off if Scourton were still on the field, but they may be in better shape than we all thought with Umanmielen stepping up for his own potential breakout year. title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 20 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 21: Christian McCaffrey #22 of the Carolina Panthers is introduced prior to the game against the Washington Football Team at Bank of America Stadium on November 21, 2021 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #20. Christian McCaffrey Panthers stats: 64 games, 3,980 rush yards, 32 TDs; 3,292 receiving yards, 18 TDs ; 1X Pro Bowl, 1X All-Pro Career stats: 112 games, 7,589 rush yards, 62 TDs; 5,390 receiving yards, 36 TDs ; 4X Pro Bowl, 3X All-Pro For many Panthers fans, Christian McCaffrey is like an ex-love interest we once dated, nearly married, then sadly watched the relationship deteriorate, then end. But four years later we are still scrolling through their Instagram, bumping into them occasionally in our shared social circles, wistfully remembering the good times, and tormenting ourselves with “what if?” Christian, we miss you. We cherished our time together. We’re happy for you that you’ve been able to move on and are flourishing in San Francisco, but deep down inside we wish you were still here. We wish that we had the football equivalent relationship of marriage, 2.2 kids, and a house with a white picket fence on Mint Street. Alas, what could have been. Christian McCaffrey was one of the most exciting and productive players to ever play for the Carolina Panthers. He was the team’s first round pick, No. 8 overall, in the 2017 draft after a stellar college career at Stanford. Carolina brought him along slowly as a runner in his 2017 rookie campaign. Running back Jonathan Stewart and quarterback Cam Newton did most of the heavy lifting with between-the-tackles running, but even then over 16 games McCaffrey still had 117 carries for 435 yards and two touchdowns. But where he excelled was as a pass catcher, reeling in 80 receptions for 651 yards and five scores. It was obvious early on that the Panthers had landed a lethal dual-threat dynamo. In his 2018 sophomore season he rushed for 1,098 yards with 867 receiving yards on 107 receptions and 13 total touchdowns as the Panthers went 7-9. He earned All-Pro Second Team honors but missed the Pro Bowl. In 2019 McCaffrey absolutely dominated the NFL. He rushed for 1,387 yards while averaging 4.8 yards per carry and scoring 15 touchdowns. He reeled in 116 receptions for 1,005 yards and four more scores as the Panthers went 5-11. He was a Pro Bowler, All-Pro First Team, and placed third in the Offensive Player of the Year voting. Among his accolades listed on the Panthers website , he was the fastest player in NFL history to reach 3,000 rushing and receiving yards. His 116 receptions were the most ever by a running back. He became just the third player in league history with 1,000 rushing and receiving yards in the same season. His 2,392 scrimmage yards in 2019 ranks No. 3 in NFL history. True, the Panthers went just 12-20 in McCaffrey’s two dominant seasons in 2018 and 2019, but the lack of team success wasn’t CMC’s fault. Plus, McCaffrey appeared durable after appearing in every one of the Panthers 48 games over his first three seasons. It looked like he would be a Carolina Panther for life, elevate the team to future glory, then ride off to the Hall of Fame. And then things took a regrettable turn in 2020 and 2021. Injuries plagued CMC over those two years and he appeared in just 10 total games. And the Panthers kept losing, going 10-23 as the franchise aimlessly cycled between quarterbacks and coaching staffs. Despite all of this, Carolina extended McCaffrey in 2020 on a four-year, $64 million deal, indicating their long-term commitment to the team’s only viable offensive weapon and fan favorite. The 2022 season began much as the seasons before it had, with too many Panthers losses. Carolina was 1-5 to begin the year but a now-healthy CMC was still his versatile, dominant self with 670 scrimmage yards on a terrible offense. And then the Panthers shockingly traded him mid-season to the San Francisco 49ers for a discount variety pack of “meh” draft picks in the second, third, fourth, and fifth rounds. Since joining the 49ers during the 2022 season, McCaffrey has been flat-out dominant. His 2024 campaign was limited to four games due to injury, but outside of that he has been an All-Pro First Team player and Top 5 MVP candidate. As Panthers fans, most of us still root for Christian McCaffrey and fondly remember the good old days when the generational dual-threat running back lit up the scoreboard in Carolina. Many of us wish he was still here. If only there had been more winning. If only he had been able to stay healthy. If only the front office and ownership hadn’t been so inept. If only.

title: Bears 53-man roster predictions: Week 2 preseason edition
summary: We’re two preseason games into the three-game 2026 preseason, and the Chicago Bears are inching closer towards the final decisions that go into making the 53-man roster. Players currently on the 90-man squad have one last game to stake their claim on a spot on the active roster. Considering most of the spots on the […]
full_text: We’re two preseason games into the three-game 2026 preseason, and the Chicago Bears are inching closer towards the final decisions that go into making the 53-man roster. Players currently on the 90-man squad have one last game to stake their claim on a spot on the active roster. Considering most of the spots on the team are essentially set in stone, though, there are only a single-digit amount of roster spots that are realistically up for grabs. For the sake of predictability, these roster projections don’t take into account the possibility of the Bears claiming anybody off of waivers, nor do they take into account the possibility they sign somebody from a different team to join their practice squad. It’s highly likely at least one of those two outcomes will happen, but with over 1,000 new free agents hitting the market, it would be impossible to predict which players Chicago should add. Without further ado, these are my updated projections for the Bears’ 53-man roster. QB (3): Caleb Williams, Tyson Bagent, Case Keenum I’m not expecting any change from the Bears’ quarterback room last year. The only other quarterback currently on the team is Miller Moss, and he hasn’t performed well enough in the preseason to usurp Case Keenum for that third-string spot. RB (3): D’Andre Swift, Kyle Monangai, Roschon Johnson The Bears carried four running backs on their roster last year, but they don’t have a special teams ace in the bunch like they had with Travis Homer in 2025. If they keep a fourth running back on the team, though, I’d keep an eye on Salvon Ahmed. He had a special teams tackle against the Bengals on Saturday and is averaging 6.6 yards per carry to Brittain Brown’s 1.4. WR (6): Rome Odunze, Luther Burden III, Kalif Raymond, Jahdae Walker, Zavion Thomas, Scotty Miller Barring injury, the Bears’ top five wide receiver spots seem pretty locked in. The real question is which player will take that WR6 spot, if Chicago even employs six receivers on the 53-man roster at all. In my opinion, Kaden Davis has looked the best of the remaining receivers when you factor in receiving ability and special teams value. However, Davis also has practice squad eligibility, whereas players like Scotty Miller or Maurice Alexander would eat into how many veterans they’re allowed to have on the practice squad. I have Miller making the cut for his special teams value, though if you wanted to put Davis here, I wouldn’t complain at all. TE (4): Colston Loveland, Cole Kmet, Sam Roush, Hayden Large With the anticipation that the Bears will run more 13 personnel in 2026, it would make sense for them to keep four tight ends on the roster. They’ll need to keep that element of their offensive game plan in tact if one of Colston Loveland, Cole Kmet, or Sam Roush go down with an injury. My choice for the TE4 role is Hayden Large, who has put together some solid run-blocking tape while tallying two special teams tackles against the Browns in the Bears’ preseason opener. OT (4): Ozzy Trapilo, Darnell Wright, Braxton Jones, Theo Benedet With Ozzy Trapilo likely to be ready for Week 1, at least one of Jedrick Wills Jr. or Kiran Amegadjie will be on the outside looking in on the Bears’ 53-man roster. They won’t keep six offensive tackles on the roster, but there’s no guarantee they’ll keep five offensive tackles on the team, either. Braxton Jones makes the cut as a backup due to his contract, while Theo Benedet has outperformed the other backup tackles on the roster this preseason, in my opinion. OG (4): Joe Thuney, Jonah Jackson, Luke Newman, Jordan McFadden There aren’t any real surprises with the Bears’ guard group. There’s a chance that Caden “Vanilla Gorilla” Barnett could make the cut here as a backup, but Chicago might like its chances of retaining him on the practice squad. Luke Newman and Jordan McFadden have shown in flashes that they can be solid backups at the next level. C (2): Garrett Bradbury, Logan Jones This one’s chalk. Garrett Bradbury is the Bears’ projected starting center in Week 1, while Logan Jones was their second-round pick this year. There’s nothing to see here. DE (5): Montez Sweat, Dayo Odeyingbo, Austin Booker, Daniel Hardy, Marcus Davenport If Shemar Turner is in a good enough spot to make the Bears’ 53-man roster, he’ll have a spot on the team. However, he’s still on the PUP list as of this writing, and rather than project when he’ll be healthy by without having that information, I’ll play it safe. Marcus Davenport is coming off a rough year with the Lions, during which he placed No. 118 among 120 qualified NFL edge rushers in PFN EDGE Impact Scoring , but his experience with Dennis Allen’s system could make him a serviceable stopgap EDGE5 until Turner comes back. If you want to reward Jamree Kromah with a roster spot for his performance this preseason, I’d be totally on board. I just have him on the practice squad because he has no eligibility restrictions there. DT (5): Gervon Dexter Sr., Grady Jarrett, Neville Gallimore, Jordan van den Berg, Kentavius Street These first three defensive tackles are set in stone, and Jordan van den Berg has been too good in training camp and the preseason to not make the Bears’ 53-man roster. Kentavius Street finds himself on the fringe of making the squad with van den Berg’s strong play recently, but he’s still listed as one of Chicago’s second-string defensive tackles. That may not mean anything, but to me, it shows he could be decent bet to make the 53-man squad. LB (5): Devin Bush, T.J. Edwards, D’Marco Jackson, Jack Sanborn, Ruben Hyppolite II Injuries to Noah Sewell and Keyshaun Elliott should leave these five linebackers in a safe spot to make the Bears’ roster. Once both of them come back healthy, general manager Ryan Poles will have some tough decisions to make. Personally, I think Sewell would be the one linebacker of the aforementioned seven who would find himself on the way out, though Hyppolite was shaky in the Bengals game after a strong outing against Cleveland. CB (5): Jaylon Johnson, Tyrique Stevenson, Malik Muhammad, Terell Smith, Josh Blackwell It feels like there’s no end in sight to the Kyler Gordon saga in Chicago. Solely because of a lack of transparency around the situation, I don’t feel comfortable projecting him to come off the PUP list. This would likely slide Malik Muhammad inside as the Bears’ starting nickel cornerback, though Josh Blackwell and safety Cam Lewis could compete for snaps, as well. Terell Smith feels like a safe bet to make the team after missing all of 2025 due to injury. S (4): Dillon Thieneman, Xavier Woods, Cam Lewis, Jaylon Jones Jaylon Jones is currently listed as a safety on the Bears’ depth chart, and though he’s taken most of his NFL snaps as an outside cornerback, that positional versatility could help him make the 53-man roster. Injuries to Coby Bryant and Elijah Hicks have Chicago thin at safety, so if Jones could take snaps there, he’d be a safe bet to make the team, having appeared in 15 games for the team last year. ST (3): Cairo Santos, Tory Taylor, Beau Gardner These three players are the only specialists the Bears have on the roster. There’s an outside chance they could look for a new long snapper on the waiver wire — Beau Gardner had a bad snap on Cairo Santos’ missed field goal against the Browns, after all — but since I’m not projecting outside additions here, this is what you get. title: Building Glass Houses: Chicago’s Fragile Defensive Line
summary: By and large, teams will build their starting rosters and their meaningful depth out of the first three rounds of the draft. The rate of investment league-wide in “defensive linemen” (here including edge-rushers of both types, defensive ends of various styles, and all defensive tackles) is going to hover around 24 of these “premium” picks […]
full_text: By and large, teams will build their starting rosters and their meaningful depth out of the first three rounds of the draft. The rate of investment league-wide in “defensive linemen” (here including edge-rushers of both types, defensive ends of various styles, and all defensive tackles) is going to hover around 24 of these “premium” picks per draft class, understanding that some classifications will always be open for debate depending on how players are utilized. Just to keep up with the league average, though, over the last five years the Bears should have invested 3.75 premium picks on the line. Chic ago Bears general manager Ryan Poles has done more or less that, even if he has been on the cheaper end of that scale. He drafted Gervon Dexter (#53), Zacch Pickens (#64), and Shemar Turner (#62)–while also trading a 2nd-round pick for Montez Sweat (#40). He also spent another four non-premium picks on the line: Dominique Robinson, Travis Bell, Austin Booker, and Jordan van den Berg. That is eight picks in five years, suggesting a non-negligible amount of attention. Except it’s important to remember that two defensive linemen were also traded away (Khalil Mack and Robert Quinn) for a 2nd-round pick, a 4th-round pick, and a 6th-round pick. So, when considering investments he “cashed out”, Poles actually only invested a net of 3 premium picks in the defensive line and two other picks, or roughly one per year. That is a below-average level of investment, and that should be concerning. Here, based on historical trend data, is how many disruptive plays per game each of those draft picks should be expected to provide. In this case, a disruption is considered any play that wins the down for the defense (a batted pass, a sack, or a tackle for a loss). There is a notable skew favoring the top of the draft, where Poles has not invested any picks, and then fairly consistent diminishing returns that match virtually any metric used to track draft picks. Still, a chart like the previous one tends to overlook nuance within rounds. Here, instead, is what things look like from the second half of the first round through the top of the fourth round. On average, one of the least efficient places to invest in the defensive line is at the end of the second round and again at the end of the third round. All three of the “premium” picks invested directly by Poles in the defensive happen to be in that first “dip” at 49-64, and although Poles has had available three picks in the “rebound” range of 65-80, all three have instead been spent on offensive players (Velus Jones, Kiran Amegadjie, and Sam Roush). Now, to be clear, these are general trends gathered from 2011-2020, and so there is plenty of room to question the applicability of this data to any individual selection. However, if I knew nothing about the individual players taken and simply had this data, I would expect to find a defensive line that lacked defensive playmakers. What results did he actually get with those picks? Well, Gervon Dexter is roughly on-track for his draft position, Zacch Pickens underperformed for his draft position, and Shemar Turner has been a non-entity so far due to injury. So while Montez Sweat is providing per-game disruption almost exactly in line with a pick from the first 11 spots in the draft (1.37, when the mean is 1.31 and the median is 1.22) and Austin Booker is in fact playing like a second-round pick on a per-game basis, the rest of the defensive line is not making up for the lack of investment. Dexter and Robinson are more or less the players they should have been, Booker is roughly the player that Pickens should have been, and Pickens was essentially aspiring to meet the standards of a 7th-round pick (and failing at that). While it is dangerous to start compounding math and trying to derive too many secondary values, once Sweat is excluded the draft picks Chicago has spent on the defensive line are producing roughly 80-85% of the per-game disruption that would be expected of the already meager draft investment. Notably, however, these numbers all refer to rate of performance, and that hides the loss of value from Travis Bell and Zacch Pickens both playing in fewer games than their draft position would suggest, and it ignores the unfortunate reality that Shemar Turner has already missed half of all of the playing time available to him due to injury. That’s not the entire story, because there is also the matter of free agency. Poles has brought in eight players in free agency whose contracts were significant enough to impact the compensatory pick formula, and a ninth (Yannick Ngakoue) whose pay was in that level even if he personally did not qualify. Collectively, these players have been signed for contracts for 204 games to date, and they provided 51.5 disruptive plays in those games (or 0.25 disruptions per contracted game). If that seems like a deceptively negative way of phrasing it, then it’s also possible to say that Ryan Poles has contracted for 10.3 disruptions per season. Given that in 2025 alone, that level of production was matched by roughly two defensive linemen per team , the simple and unavoidable reality is that free agency does not provide a “cover” for the draft inadequacies of the Bears over the last five years. Chicago has built a house with glass walls, with a defensive line that resembles the level of priority it has been given over the last five years—and even there, the majority of its (relative) success rests upon a single trade and a fifth-round player making up for what is otherwise mediocrity and underperformance. The draft selections most likely to have been able to cover this lack with relative efficiency were instead spent elsewhere, often on players who also disappointed relative to draft status. Free agency has not been the answer. Something, ultimately, will need to give—and it will likely be the Bears at the line of scrimmage .

They handily defeated the Bears — who played their starters for a short period of time while the Bengals didn’t — by a score of 27-9. title: What comes next as the Bengals’ search for a swing tackle continues?
summary: After a 0.0 PFF pass-blocking grade on Saturday night against the Chicago Bears, Cody Ford was released by the Cincinnati Bengals on Monday. Ford had been active in 50 out of 51 games since joining the Bengals, playing mostly on special teams units. He also had filled in at four different spots on the offensive […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals guard Cody Ford (61), left and Cincinnati Bengals center Trey Hill (63), right, block Tampa Bay Buccaneers defensive tackle C.J. Brewer (95) in the first quarter of the NFL preseason game at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati on Saturday, August 10, 2024. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co After a 0.0 PFF pass-blocking grade on Saturday night against the Chicago Bears, Cody Ford was released by the Cincinnati Bengals on Monday. Ford had been active in 50 out of 51 games since joining the Bengals, playing mostly on special teams units. He also had filled in at four different spots on the offensive line throughout the years. With much better depth on the interior of the offensive line in 2026, Ford needed to prove that he could be a reliable swing tackle option. The writing seemed on the wall when the Bengals suddenly moved Jalen Rivers back outside to tackle. After the performance Saturday, the Bengals decided to go ahead and release Ford now. This is likely a show of respect for his years of service, giving him the opportunity to find a new team before the chaos of cut-down day. After the Bengals released Ford, head coach Zac Taylor briefly touched on the competition at swing tackle and sounded open to finding one who is currently not on the roster. “I think we’re always open to everything,” Taylor said. “These guys are really competing. I feel like I’d like to see someone grab it and us be able to say that. But certainly, with time still in the practice, we got some stuff to sort out.” Of the current options on the roster, the Bengals could opt to keep working Rivers as a swing tackle, hoping that more snaps help him become more comfortable on the outside of the offensive line. He played a good amount of left tackle at Miami in college. They could also give Brian Parker a chance to work more at the spot. Or they could go with Javon Foster at the position. Foster graded out with a 61.8 on Saturday night in pass protection, along with a 73.5 run-blocking grade. While his kick-slide in pass protection looks a bit stiff, he generally does a good enough job with his hands to maintain control of the man in front of him. The former fourth-round selection by the Jaguars has yet to play in a regular-season game in his young career. Javon Foster took snaps at both left and right tackle versus Detroit. pic.twitter.com/KwcvGLkA94 — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) August 16, 2026 The Bengals may look outside the roster, depending on what happens in cuts across the league. They could opt to put in a waiver claim this weekend, when teams around the league cut down to 53-man rosters.

title: Positive injury update on Bryan Cook and Dax Hill
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals‘ revamped defense has looked impressive through the first two preseason games, but there are still a couple of important pieces waiting to get back on the field. Safety Bryan Cook and defensive back Dax Hill have both been sidelined during the preseason, leaving Cincinnati without two players expected to play significant roles […]
full_text: Jun 16, 2026; Cincinnati, OH, USA; Cincinnati Bengals safety Bryan Cook (6) runs with the ball during minicamp at Kettering Health Practice Fields. Mandatory Credit: Katie Stratman-Imagn Images | Katie Stratman-Imagn Images The Cincinnati Bengals ‘ revamped defense has looked impressive through the first two preseason games, but there are still a couple of important pieces waiting to get back on the field. Safety Bryan Cook and defensive back Dax Hill have both been sidelined during the preseason, leaving Cincinnati without two players expected to play significant roles in the secondary. Head coach Zac Taylor provided an update on both players Monday as the Bengals begin their final week of preseason preparation. The good news is that neither situation appears to be trending toward a long-term absence. Zac Taylor speaks to the media. https://t.co/xDv8Tw8EYv — Cincinnati Bengals (@Bengals) August 24, 2026 Taylor: Cook and Hill are progressing Taylor was asked about Cook and Hill and whether either player could return to practice this week. “They’re progressing,” Taylor said. “They started running a little bit more on the side of the rehab field, so I won’t put a timeline on it. But encouraged by the progress that they’re making.” That’s essentially the same message the Bengals have been sending throughout the preseason: Progress, but no timetable, at least for Hill. That’s because Cook was present for Monday’s practice but did not do team drills, while Hill remains out. Bryan Cook back at Bengals practice Monday pic.twitter.com/2ZvdopWVyD — Mike Petraglia (@Trags) August 24, 2026 Bryan Cook isn’t doing team drills in his first day back, looks like they’ll ease him back into things — Kelsey Conway (@KelseyLConway) August 24, 2026 Before today, both players had been working on the rehab field rather than participating in full team practices. Cook suffered what is believed to be a minor soft-tissue hamstring injury during a stadium practice earlier this month, while Hill has been dealing with what has been described as overall hamstring tightness. Neither injury was initially believed to be serious. The fact that both are now increasing their running activity is certainly encouraging. Cincinnati has been cautious with both players The Bengals haven’t had much reason to push either player. Taylor ruled both Cook and Hill out of the preseason opener against Detroit, and neither returned for the second preseason game against Chicago. Instead, Cincinnati has used the extra preseason opportunities to evaluate the players competing for depth roles behind them. That approach has worked out reasonably well. The Bengals’ defense was particularly impressive against Chicago, holding the Bears without a touchdown in a 27-9 Cincinnati victory despite the Bengals sitting their starters. The performance provided more evidence that Cincinnati has considerably more depth on defense than it did a year ago. But getting Cook and Hill back would still represent a significant boost. Cook was one of Cincinnati’s major offseason additions, returning to the organization after spending the previous two seasons in Kansas City. Hill, meanwhile, enters an important season as the Bengals’ fifth-year option player and is expected to be a key piece of the secondary. The timing is worth watching With the Bengals’ preseason finale against Philadelphia coming Friday, neither player will likely play in that game. And considering Taylor’s cautious approach throughout the preseason, Cincinnati has little incentive to rush either player back merely to get some exhibition snaps. The more important question is whether Cook and Hill can get back onto the practice field soon enough to be fully prepared for Week 1. For now, Taylor’s message is a positive one. They’re running more. They’re progressing. And, most importantly, there haven’t been indications that either injury is becoming something more serious. For a Bengals defense that has generated plenty of optimism this summer following the additions of players such as Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen and Kyle Dugger, getting two of its projected starters back healthy could make the unit even more dangerous. Now it’s just a matter of when Cook and Hill are ready to make their return.

title: Bengals News: Could Dan Pitcher eventually take play-calling duties from Zac Taylor?
summary: It was a fun preseason game against the Chicago Bears for the Cincinnati Bengals. And some may have noticed things looked a bit different from the offense, but may not have been able to put their finger on it. Well it turns out that head coach Zac Taylor let offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher an opportunity […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher looks on during the Cincinnati Bengals practice in Cincinnati on Tuesday, May 27, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co It was a fun preseason game against the Chicago Bears for the Cincinnati Bengals. And some may have noticed things looked a bit different from the offense, but may not have been able to put their finger on it. Well it turns out that head coach Zac Taylor let offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher an opportunity to call plays. Truly it was very smart to test this out in this setting. You get a real game time experience of going through the logistics. It was also a chance to give this offense a breath of fresh air after Taylor has called plays since arriving. “Pitch did an excellent job. Before the game tonight, he did an excellent job,” Taylor told Geoff Hobson of Bengals.com. “Great prep all week, preparing for this practice, (then) calling the game. I know he had a great feel for it. So, I thought he did an excellent job.” … Zac Taylor gave play-calling duties to Dan Pitcher for preseason game Bengals News Roster Look: After Dominating Bears, Bengals Salute Tight Position Battles “They’re prepared, really veteran play callers in all three phases,” Zac Taylor said. “I mean, it’s about as veteran as you get. Ben has called plays for a long time. (Special teams coordinator) Richard Hightower’s been there for a long time. DA (DC Dennis Allen) has done it forever. So, that was just good for our coaching staff, for our players to go against that. It was a good test for us all week.” The tight end position will make some very tough cuts. It may become who they think they can get back onto their practice squad. Tanner Hudson, despite being a trusted veteran, may be the odd man out. Enough younger guys behind him look like they are deserving of a spot and Hudson is getting up there in age. Bengals are a viable landing spot for veteran tackle amid latest o-line concerns Bleacher Report’s Kristopher Knox recently released his remaining bargain free agents and named offensive tackle Cam Robinson as a player who could end up with the Bengals. The Bengals desperately need more depth behind their starters and Cam Robinson could very well be that guy. In a dream scenario maybe, but more likely they will stick with the rank and file. Then we will have to hope the Bengals do not need more help. Bengals’ OL problems could show up big on final cuts While the Bengals return all five starters on the line for the first time in the Joe Burrow era, the depth behind those first on the chart looks shaky. It will be interesting to see who falls off the team. It will be something to watch if they find a replacement behind the current starters. Maybe it is time to cut ties with a veteran or disappointing pick. NFL News Predicting NFL teams most likely to improve in 2026 season Even by NFL standards, 2025 was a topsy-turvy season. Seven teams saw their records improve or decline by at least six wins, the most in any campaign since 2008. And though that’s a little more feasible in a 17-game season than it was in the 16-game era, the 10-game improvement by the Patriots, who improved from 4-13 to 14-3, was the largest by any team since 1999, when the Colts pulled that off in Peyton Manning’s second season. The Bengals not being on the list is a bit surprising. It makes a bit of sense since the other teams missed the playoffs severely more. 2026 NFL Roster Cuts: Predicting the Biggest Names Who Could Hit the Market Every year, there are some surprising departures. Some are early-round picks who just haven’t panned out, veterans who are released as much for economics as performance, and aging vets at the end of the line. Maybe a name or two in here could be a potential improvement in certain areas, but no one here seems to be a quality add to any depth. View this post on Instagram Yikes dog. Not great after he expressed serious frustration with the fans. It makes sense that the dude getting paid the most will be trotted out there to try and salvage the move that mortgaged the franchise.

title: Evan McPherson is putting together a statement in training camp and preseason for the Bengals
summary: There was a time when Evan McPherson making a 50-plus-yard field goal barely registered as news. That was the expectation. The Bengals’ kicker had established himself as one of the NFL’s most dangerous long-range weapons, and there was a stretch early in his career when anything from beyond midfield felt almost automatic. He was incredible […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals kicker Evan McPherson (2) celebrates with Cincinnati Bengals punter Kevin Huber (10) after hitting the game winning field goal in overtime of the AFC championship NFL football game, Sunday, Jan. 30, 2022, at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Mo. Cincinnati Bengals defeated Kansas City Chiefs 27-24. Cincinnati Bengals At Kansas City Chiefs Jan 30 Afc Championship 105 There was a time when Evan McPherson making a 50-plus-yard field goal barely registered as news. That was the expectation. The Bengals’ kicker had established himself as one of the NFL’s most dangerous long-range weapons, and there was a stretch early in his career when anything from beyond midfield felt almost automatic. He was incredible as a rookie in the team’s 2021 run to Super Bowl LVI, and became one of the best young kickers in the league. After a couple of uneven seasons, however, McPherson entered 2026 with something to prove. So far, he’s doing exactly that. McPherson continued his outstanding training camp and preseason Saturday night against the Chicago Bears, drilling both of his field-goal attempts—including a 58-yarder—and all three of his extra-point attempts in Cincinnati’s second preseason game. And that 58-yarder? It looked extremely easy, and Mike Watts on the Bengals preseason telecast referenced “Thor’s Hammer” when referring to McPherson’s leg. McPherson is making long kicks look routine again The Bengals’ first preseason game against Detroit already provided a glimpse of what McPherson could be bringing to the 2026 season. He connected on a 56-yard field goal in Cincinnati’s 16-14 victory, then added kicks from 33 and 41 yards. That performance pushed him to 29-for-31 on field-goal attempts in his preseason career at the time. Saturday night against Chicago, McPherson picked up right where he left off. His he hit field goals from 58 yards, and from 25, while also converting all three of his extra-point attempts. That’s an awfully good night for a kicker, but the more important story is the consistency McPherson has shown throughout the summer. This hasn’t been a case of one big kick suddenly appearing out of nowhere. The training camp signs have been impossible to miss McPherson has been routinely showing off his leg during camp. Earlier this month, he made a 65-yard field goal during Cincinnati’s Friday night stadium practice, with Bengals.com noting that the kick appeared to have plenty of distance to spare. McPherson estimated afterward that he probably could have made a kick from 68 or 69 yards under those conditions. Then, just days before Saturday night’s game against Chicago, McPherson drilled a 50-yard kick through the uprights during a situational practice in which the goal posts had been narrowed to only nine feet. That isn’t simply making field goals. That’s a kicker repeatedly demonstrating that his leg is in an excellent place. And Saturday night’s Week 2 preseason game against the Bears provided another opportunity to translate that practice success into a game environment. The 58-yarder was particularly impressive There is something different about watching a kicker hit a 58-yarder in a preseason game. It’s not a meaningless extra point. It’s not a short field goal that a team would be disappointed to miss. It’s a kick that requires excellent operation from the snap and hold, along with the confidence to let the kicker attack the ball. McPherson did exactly that. The Bengals’ official video showed the 58-yarder sailing through the uprights with plenty of room to spare. It was a similar scenario with the 56-yarder in the preseason opener last week. So, it’s becoming a familiar sight again. McPherson owns the Bengals’ franchise record with a 63-yard field goal, which he set during the 2025 season. He also owns seven of Cincinnati’s nine longest field goals in franchise history. The leg has never really been the question. The consistency, at times, has. And that’s where this summer has been so encouraging. McPherson is coming off his best season There’s another reason to be optimistic about what we’re seeing. McPherson’s 2025 season was arguably the best regular-season campaign of his career. He went 25-for-28 on field goals (89.3%), including his career-long 63-yarder, while continuing to provide Cincinnati with the kind of range that changes how an offense can approach the end of a drive. That season appears to have carried into the offseason and training camp. Rather than treating 2025 as an isolated bounce-back year, McPherson is looking like a kicker who has found something in his operation and consistency. And for a Bengals team that has Super Bowl aspirations, that’s a pretty significant development. The Bengals need this version of Evan McPherson It’s easy to overlook the importance of a reliable kicker when a team has Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins on offense. But Cincinnati has experienced firsthand how valuable McPherson can be. Field goals matter. Close games matter. Late-game situations matter. And when a team is trying to make a deep postseason run, having a kicker who can comfortably hit from 50-plus yards can change the way coaches call games. A drive that stalls around the opponent’s 40-yard line doesn’t necessarily have to end in a punt. A quarterback doesn’t have to force a throw into coverage simply because the offense didn’t get all the way into the red zone. The Bengals can trust McPherson to give them points. And if he’s consistently connecting from 50-plus yards, that field-goal range becomes even larger. ‘Money Mac’ might be back There is still plenty of preseason football to play, and nobody should declare a kicker’s season based on training camp and two exhibition games. But it’s difficult not to like what the Bengals are seeing. McPherson has been routinely making long kicks in practice. He hit a 56-yarder against Detroit, 58-yarder against Chicago. He has also made his shorter attempts, and he’s been perfect on his extra points in the preseason. Most importantly, he looks confident—especially coming off of that career 2025 campaign. That’s the version of Evan McPherson Cincinnati needs. The Bengals didn’t draft McPherson in the fifth round of the 2021 NFL Draft expecting him to merely be an adequate kicker. They drafted him because he could be a weapon. For much of his career, he has been exactly that. Now, after some inconsistency in the middle portion of his career, McPherson appears to be rediscovering that same swagger. And if what we’ve seen throughout training camp and the first two preseason games carries into September, the Bengals may once again have one of the NFL’s most dangerous weapons sitting on the other side of the line of scrimmage. The Bengals have questions to answer before Week 1. Evan McPherson doesn’t look like one of them.

title: The Bengals may be ready to find a new swing tackle
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals handily defeated the Chicago Bears on Saturday night, going to 2-0 in the preseason so far, by a score of 27-9. The defense kept the Bears out of the end zone throughout the entire game — even though the Bears’ starters played while the Bengals benched theirs — and both Josh Johnson […]
full_text: Dec 28, 2025; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Cincinnati Bengals guard Cody Ford (61) leaves the field after a game against the Arizona Cardinals at Paycor Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Katie Stratman-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Cincinnati Bengals handily defeated the Chicago Bears on Saturday night, going to 2-0 in the preseason so far, by a score of 27-9. The defense kept the Bears out of the end zone throughout the entire game — even though the Bears’ starters played while the Bengals benched theirs — and both Josh Johnson and Sean Clifford were able to score touchdowns. They may have an offensive line problem. though. It’s not with their starters—Orlando Brown Jr, Dylan Fairchild, Ted Karras, Dalton Risner, and Amarius Mims are set and did not play in Week 2 of the preseason. They have an issue with their backup offensive linemen. Over the last three years, Cody Ford has been the team’s swing tackle, though he has played every position on the line save center. He started at right guard for the Bengals on Saturday night, and he struggled (especially in pass protection, earning a 0.0 from PFF). And it hasn’t just been this game either. Based on multiple reports, Ford has had an inconsistent camp at best, and obviously hasn’t inspired trust that he can back up Brown and Mims—both of whom are big guys and have missed games for the Bengals in the past. The Cincinnati Enquirer’s Kelsey Conway was able to discuss the issue with head coach Zac Taylor, and he said no decisions have been made. “I think that’s still pretty open,” he said, per Conway . “I think there’s guys we’re still looking at, and I wouldn’t say there’s any decision we’ve made there.” The Bengals have done so well this offseason when it comes to reshaping the defense. They added Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen, Bryan Cook, and others, and they added some talent in the draft as well. What they didn’t do was address the offensive line. Hopefully, whoever they decide earns the job doesn’t even need to step on the field, but they need to do something before the season starts. Luckily, there is going to be a large number of cuts made soon, and there’s bound to be someone they could sign as their swing tackle. Or, if they want to be more proactive, they could look at making another trade to bring in a backup offensive tackle. Hopefully they just do something.
