title: Lions preseason film breakdown: Juice Scruggs makes case for starting role
summary: The Detroit Lions need someone to reliably hold down the center position until starter Cade Mays recovers from his wrist injury. Juice Scruggs made his case on Saturday afternoon against the Washington Commanders in the Lions’ second game of the 2026 preseason. Despite some promising play from Seth McLaughlin in training camp, the competition may […]
full_text: The Detroit Lions need someone to reliably hold down the center position until starter Cade Mays recovers from his wrist injury. Juice Scruggs made his case on Saturday afternoon against the Washington Commanders in the Lions’ second game of the 2026 preseason. Despite some promising play from Seth McLaughlin in training camp, the competition may be over. Let’s take a moment to give credit where credit is due. Lions General Manager Brad Holmes notably got a strong return in the offseason trade of former Lions running back David Montgomery, a package that not only included the 2026 fourth-round pick but also the versatile interior offensive lineman. When asked about Scruggs , the 2023 second-round pick out of Penn State, Holmes described his fit on the roster: “His makeup and all the intangible qualities that he possesses, we were all blown away by that coming out of the draft process. So just to see actual tangible evidence of him starting both guard spots, starting center, and actually holding his own at all three, it was impressive.” With Holmes’ strong track record as an evaluator for the NFL Draft, it is worth looking back on what draft experts said about Scruggs at the time. The Athletic’s Dane Brugler wrote the following strengths for Scruggs in his The Beast draft profile : “plays on high alert to read stunts/twists … uses the strength in his arms and upper body to finish in the run game … shows accurate timing release on combos and second-level blocks … team captain and was the veteran voice in Penn State’s offensive line room” Scruggs checks the boxes of a Holmes draft pick, as the fit and vision are clear. Scruggs is the type of player who can step in anywhere along the interior offensive line when the inevitable injury over the course of an NFL season occurs. Let’s take a look at how these strengths were displayed on the field. Strong at the second level Scruggs repeatedly showed his ability to climb to the second level with effort and physicality. Let’s start with what I view as Scruggs’s strongest rep of the game. The Lions run a duo run scheme (video below), where Scruggs (No. 70) first attacks the 2i-technique with left guard Christian Mahogany and then, with accurate timing and release, moves up to block the second-level defender. He not only succeeds with his assignment, but also plays the rep with high effort, physicality, and finish. This is the kind of play that builds trust from the coaching staff. On this next example, Scruggs works a combination block with right guard Tate Ratledge. Together, they drive the nose tackle off the line of scrimmage until Scruggs releases off to engage with the second-level linebacker. Now Scruggs has repeated the concept to both his left and right, banking on trust. Flashing functional athleticism Versatility in the run game has been a staple for the Dan Campbell era of Lions football. However, an offense is limited if players are better suited to one particular scheme than another. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing discussed the importance of adaptability to build an offense around the players you have . While the first two plays spotlighted above feature a duo blocking scheme, the next play below is a wide-zone design. Scruggs flashes functional athleticism to get the snap off and successfully reach-block the 1- technique. If Scruggs can consistently play well in multiple run-game looks like he did against the Commanders, the Lions offense should be in good shape until Cade Mays works his way back into the lineup. Building chemistry With limited reps together so far this training camp, the interior offensive line needs to gel quickly, with the regular season rapidly approaching. We saw evidence of this early in pass protection. Notice Scruggs instinctively transition to pass off his man to Mahogany to his left and then mentally shift his attention to help Ratledge to his right. He looks controlled and confident in his movements, not scattered and questioning where his teammates are as they pick up the rush as a unit. Always room for improvement It was unquestionably a strong night for Juice Scruggs. But every coach and player will tell you there is always something to learn and grow from on tape. Below is that play. Right off the snap, Scruggs puts himself in a great position to win the rep. By reaching the 1- technique and getting his helmet across with his hips not far behind, Scruggs establishes leverage against the defender. As the play develops, it appears his feet get a bit stuck in the mud, allowing the defensive tackle to get vertical with his rush. Admittedly, this is nitpicking. Due to the run-action rollout concept, if Scruggs were to “lose” the rep, this is the best way he could have done so. And even then, it would be questionable to even record this as an allowed pressure. To hold down the center job, the Lions don’t need Juice Scruggs to be a game changer. They need him to be exactly who he is: a versatile football player who plays with instincts and physicality. Against Washington, Scruggs did exactly that. All Juice, no pulp.
author: Anthony Balaj

title: 5 key stats from Detroit Lions’ preseason win over Washington Commanders
summary: The Detroit Lions got their first win of the 2026 preseason, defeating the Washington Commanders at Ford Field, 17-13. Detroit’s defense was particularly impressive, limiting Washington’s offense to just 35 rushing yards across 17 carries, and surrendering just nine first downs over 45 plays run on offense. As we’ll do every week throughout the season […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-AUGUST 22: Detroit Lions wide receiver Jackson Meeks (13) lines up before a play during the second half of an NFL preseason football game between the Washington Commanders and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Saturday, August 22, 2026 (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The Detroit Lions got their first win of the 2026 preseason, defeating the Washington Commanders at Ford Field, 17-13. Detroit’s defense was particularly impressive, limiting Washington’s offense to just 35 rushing yards across 17 carries, and surrendering just nine first downs over 45 plays run on offense. As we’ll do every week throughout the season for this Lions team, we have data we can comb through, courtesy of Pro Football Focus, that helps us better understand the football the Lions have played thus far—and what to look forward to in the coming weeks. Let’s take a closer look at the Lions by the numbers after their preseason win over the Commanders. Pro Football Focus’ premium statistics are an invaluable data point for football fans to better understand the game. Consider subscribing to PFF to have full access to a plethora of stats and grades to keep you informed about the NFL—and college football, too. Also, NFL Pro is supplying some innovative and illustrative advanced statistics of their own that are worth checking out for the price of admission . 100.0 pass-blocking efficiency, 72.0 run-blocking grade In what we can assume to be Tate Ratledge’s only snaps of the preseason, it was a reminder of just how effective the second-year player is at this point in his career. Ratledge earned a pristine 100.0 pass-blocking efficiency score —a signature stat from Pro Football Focus that measures pressure allowed on a per-snap basis with weighting toward sacks allowed—not allowing a single pressure, hurry, quarterback hit, or sack across his seven pass-blocking snaps. After a rewatch of the tape, Ratledge was a positive force in the run game, working double teams and getting active at the second level. Among the 95 qualifying guards in the preseason’s Week 2, Ratledge’s combined score of his pass-blocking efficiency and his run grade made him PFF’s 12th-highest-rated guard of the week. 26 defensive stops As previously mentioned, the Lions defense was stifling against the Commanders. There are plenty of individual performances to highlight, including the preseason debut of Derrick Moore and the Lions debut of DJ Wonnum, both of whom picked up sacks. Skyler Gill-Howard flashed more of the disruption and playmaking that’s earned him attention and praise during training camp. The starting cornerback duo of D.J. Reed and Rock Ya-Sin allowed a combined two receptions for 9 yards. But the best way to capture just how productive the Lions defense was against the Commanders is to look at how many defensive stops they made on Saturday. While Washington ran 45 plays on offense, Detroit’s defenders combined to record 26 defensive stops —PFF’s stat that measures how many tackles constitute a “failure” for the offense. That’s a lot of failure from the Commanders, and that was all without Aidan Hutchinson, Alim McNeill, or Jack Campbell taking a snap. 20.9 passing grade under pressure Teddy Bridgewater’s sudden retirement has put the Lions in a bit of a bind at the backup quarterback position. Detroit was quick to make a move for another quarterback, signing Joshua Dobbs less than two weeks ago. We’ve seen how this coaching staff values experienced players at positions all over the field, but there’s been a clear emphasis on having the backup quarterback be a veteran. And while Dobbs’ 600+ dropbacks in the regular season and familiarity with Drew Petzing seem to make him the frontrunner for the QB2 role in Detroit, his play against the Commanders didn’t look like that of a veteran. The sack fumble on the team’s second snap of the game wasn’t entirely Dobbs’ fault after Larry Borom was beaten off the snap, but Tyler Conklin’s assignment was clearly to block any extra pressure at the LOS—which he did—and release to the flat. Dobbs didn’t diagnose the possibility of Amik Robertson blitzing—the cornerback did disguise it until the last moment—but instead of dumping the ball off to his checkdown—Conklin—Dobbs tried to roll out to his left, but ran right into the pressure of Robertson. On the next series, facing a third-and-6 from their own 45-yard line, Dobbs was guilty of trying to do too much again. After bailing on a fairly clean pocket, he launched a throw across his body to the middle of the field that sailed past his target and was easily intercepted. Reviewing the play, Tay Martin was open on a drag route at the end of Dobbs’ dropback, which likely would have resulted in a first down—or at the very least, an opportunity to go for it on fourth-and-short. All that said, Dobbs faced pressure on five of his 13 dropbacks against the Commanders, going 0-4 on those throws and earning PFF’s second-worst passing grade (20.9) for quarterbacks under pressure. By contrast, Luke Altmyer faced pressure on seven of his 17 dropbacks, completing one of his three attempts for 3 yards, choosing to eat a sack instead of committing any turnover-worthy plays. 2.75 yards per route run One celebration for the coaching staff this offseason has been the development of Jackson Meeks. Meeks’ transition from wide receiver to tight end, which started last season, has turned into a pleasant surprise for the Lions as they potentially look to increase their usage of multiple tight end sets. It might sound surprising, but through two preseason games, Meeks leads the team in receptions (5) and receiving yards (50). Against the Commanders, Meeks recorded 2.75 yards per route run , the eighth-best mark among 42 qualifying tight ends in Week 2 with at least two targets. Meeks is still in pursuit of a spot on the 53-man roster, but if he keeps making plays like his forced fumble on special teams that helped seal the win for the Lions on Saturday, it’s going to be hard to keep him from being a part of this football team come September. 5.3 yards per carry, 6.2 yards per carry To put it plainly, as it stands today, Jacob Saylors is the best running back not named Jahmyr Gibbs in Detroit. With Isiah Pacheco and Sione Vaki unable to take the field due to injury, Saylors has made the most of his opportunities through two preseason games, running the ball 14 times for 87 yards. His 5.3 yards per carry against the Commanders led the way for the four running backs who carried the ball on Saturday, but if you want to look around the league, his 6.2 yards per carry is the fourth-best mark among the 67 qualifying running backs with at least 10 carries this preseason. If you add on his 28 yards receiving, he’s seventh in total yards from scrimmage among running backs this preseason. Pacheco is the most proven runner behind Gibbs, but injuries are getting in the way for the veteran. Vaki has the most potential of this group, as his athleticism and football IQ make him a prime candidate to be the next best running back on the team, but without the reps, it makes it harder to count on Vaki with opportunities in the regular season. All of this leads back to me currently believing that Saylors is closer to being the team’s RB3 instead of RB4, thus making him a safe bet to make the 53-man roster.
author: Ryan Mathews

title: Discussion: Which Detroit Lions position group has the most uncertainty?
summary: With one preseason game left to play, the Detroit Lions will soon shift their attention towards the regular season and their initial 53-man roster. We have received some clarity on certain position battles, while others remain fiercely close. However, most of these position battles are for reserve spots, not starting positions. Part of what makes […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - AUGUST 22: Rock Ya-Sin #23 of the Detroit Lions tackles Dyami Brown #6 of the Washington Commanders during the first quarter of a preseason game at Ford Field on August 22, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images With one preseason game left to play, the Detroit Lions will soon shift their attention towards the regular season and their initial 53-man roster. We have received some clarity on certain position battles, while others remain fiercely close . However, most of these position battles are for reserve spots, not starting positions. Part of what makes predicting the roster bubble difficult is that most of these depth players need to check more boxes than just starting potential. You need versatility, you need experience, you need potential, or you need special teams prowess—some players have all three, some are struggling to find one. Looking at the starters on the team, we have a better understanding of their role on the team, but that does not mean that the Lions or their fans are overwhelmingly confident. Can the offensive and defensive lines find their form early in the season? Will the secondary hold up? How will the tertiary receiving options impact the game? There are still many questions unanswered with this roster, and we might not get answers until well into the regular season. Today’s Question of the Day is: Which Detroit Lions position group are you most unsure about? My answer: Cornerback. Right off the bat, there is the lingering question about top-end talent—are D.J. Reed and Rock Ya-Sin enough to compete in a pass-happy NFL? Yet beyond that obvious question, my biggest uncertainty is about the depth chart and how it will play out in the coming weeks. Before we get into why this is a difficult position battle to predict, we have to look at how many spots are typically available in the first place. This is how many cornerbacks and safeties that the Lions have kept on the initial 53-man roster since 2021, their first season under Dan Campbell and Brad Holmes: 2021: 6 cornerbacks, 4 safeties 2022: 6 cornerbacks, 5 safeties 2023: 7 cornerbacks, 4 safeties 2024: 6 cornerbacks, 5 safeties (initial roster had 52 players) 2025: 5 cornerbacks, 3 safeties (initial roster had 50 players; Daniel Thomas was signed during cuts, and Thomas Harper was claimed off waivers two days later) In general, the Lions have between 10 and 11 defensive backs on the roster, and I do not expect that to change in 2026. Right off the bat, we can lock in four defensive backs: D.J. Reed, Rock Ya-Sin, Christian Izien, and Keith Abney. Three more players—Chuck Clark, Thomas Harper, and Avonte Maddox—are safe bets to make the team as well. Some people may be adamant about keeping Khalil Dorsey, but the Lions love his impact on special teams. We are up to eight roster spots out of the 10 or 11 that are typical. That leaves anywhere from two to three spots for Ennis Rakestraw, Roger McCreary, and Nick Whiteside—the math checks out; it’s an easy decision, right? The biggest wrinkle is the status of safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph. It seems unlikely that either player will be ready for Week 1, but Campbell noted a few weeks ago that Branch and Joseph were making progress . If they were to stay on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list, they would be forced to miss at least four games. However, there is a non-zero chance that the Lions are encouraged by their rehab and keep one or both players on the active 53-man roster (they would need to be activated off the PUP beforehand, however). It would not be the first time that the Lions kept an injured player on the initial roster. In 2024, the Lions kept Ifeatu Melifonwu and DJ Reader on the Week 1 roster despite both nursing existing injuries. Reader returned in Week 2, while Melifonwu returned in Week 4. Detroit did the same in 2023 with Emmanuel Moseley, activating him off the PUP before cuts, although he wound up missing the first four games of the season anyway—it is worth noting that he suffered a hamstring injury during his ACL rehab. If Branch and/or Joseph are activated, then the defensive back group gets very crowded. With Branch and Joseph plus Clark, Harper, and Maddox, you have five safeties on the roster (six if you count Izien, who is projected to start at nickel). Even with those two starters back in the fold, I do not see a world in which the Lions cut one of Clark, Harper, or Maddox. Therefore, if we want to meet that estimate of 10 or 11 defensive backs, the cuts have to come from the cornerbacks. Instead of having two or three spots for Rakestraw, McCreary, and Whiteside, you would suddenly have one or two spots (keeping two plus Branch and Joseph would put the Lions at 12 defensive backs, more than they have historically done in this era). Each player has a legitimate case for a roster spot, and I frankly do not know how to approach this problem. Rakestraw has the draft pedigree, and while his career thus far has been rocky, I would be surprised to see the Lions move on from him. While I think his play has been the worst of the three, it has not been bad enough to warrant giving up on him as a prospect. As a recent second-round selection, odds are he would get claimed on waivers as well—last year, another 2023 second-rounder, JuJu Brents, was claimed off waivers after being a roster cut. Whiteside has been the biggest riser in training camp, and while his second preseason game left a lot to be desired, he has still done enough to warrant a roster spot in most situations. However, as a cornerback with limited versatility (he is predominantly an outside corner) and limited starting experience (zero career starts across 11 career games), you do have to wonder if that will hurt his roster chances. Finally, McCreary has had a quiet training camp, yet he has arguably been one of the top defenders in preseason. It might be difficult to conclude that, given his lack of interceptions and just one pass breakup, but his coverage has been tight—remember, a lack of targets usually means that his assignments are not getting open. Coupled with some solid impact as a run defender and ability to play inside or outside, his stock is rising. On one hand, keeping Branch and Joseph on the PUP is the easy solution to the problem. However, that only delays the inevitable for when they return—you will have to clear two roster spots at some point. Similarly, if they are ready to play, wouldn’t you want two Pro Bowl-caliber safeties as soon as possible? I can’t actively root for either player to stay on the PUP because of roster gymnastics. The Lions have many difficult decisions to come, but I believe that the cornerback group will be their toughest choice to make. Are they good enough? Are they happy with their depth? Only time will tell.
author: John Whiticar

title: Tyrod Taylor vs. Kyle McCord: The Case for Each Packers QB
summary: As we march towards the Green Bay Packers’ final preseason game against the Arizona Cardinals, all (some) eyes will be on the battle for the backup QB spot, which is being fought by veteran Tyrod Taylor and second-year player Kyle McCord. With starter Jordan Love missing some time in each of the previous two seasons, […]
full_text: ASHWAUBENON, WISCONSIN - JULY 31: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers talks with Tyrod Taylor #6 and Kyle McCord #18 during the Green Bay Packers training camp at Ray Nitschke Field on July 31, 2026 in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images As we march towards the Green Bay Packers’ final preseason game against the Arizona Cardinals, all (some) eyes will be on the battle for the backup QB spot, which is being fought by veteran Tyrod Taylor and second-year player Kyle McCord. With starter Jordan Love missing some time in each of the previous two seasons, the chance of the Packers QB2 seeing meaningful game action in 2026 is not zero. Today we’re going to look at the case for both QBs, and will cover the case against them later this week. The Case for Tyrod Taylor At 37 years old, Tyrod Taylor is the oldest player on the Packers roster, as well as the most experienced (16 years), both by a significant margin. Taylor has seen playing time in 101 regular-season and playoff games, starting 63 of them. For context, Jordan Love has played in 57 career NFL games. A veteran presence carries weight here—not only are you getting a guy with nearly two decades of NFL experience, but it’s almost like there’s an extra coach on offense. Through two preseason games so far, Taylor is 8/16 for 38 yards and 1 TD. Now—no sane person wants the Packers’ backup to see significant playing time this year. So if we’re trying to make the case for Taylor, maybe those numbers are fake! Preseason matters when I say it does, and right now, I’m saying preseason is fake. The Case for Kyle McCord The Packers have a QB room comprised of someone born in the ‘80s, someone born in the ‘90s, and someone born in the ‘00s, and I think that’s neat. At just 23 years old, Kyle McCord has seen zero NFL action outside of preseason, after spending time on the practice squad of the Philadelphia Eagles last year. He’s raw, but Matt LaFleur can fix him, right? After all, Jordan Love has morphed into a top 10 (argue with your mother) quarterback in the league. LaFleur can help develop another! McCord is also playing significantly better than Taylor so far this preseason, with 24 completions on 35 attempts for 220 yards. Preseason matters when I say it does, and right now, I’m saying preseason matters. — How do you feel about the backup quarterback position? Sound off in the comments section. Join the conversation! title: Packers Training Camp Recap: Final open practice before the Cardinals come to town
summary: The Green Bay Packers had about a two-hour practice on Monday that got a chippy at the end. The first fight started between receiver Matthew Golden and edge defender Barryn Sorrell, two Texas Longhorns who were brought to the Packers via last year’s draft. According to reports from the press, linebacker Zaire Franklin and edge […]
full_text: Players including Marshawn Lloyd #32 and Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers participate in a drill during training camp at Ray Nitschke Field in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin, on August 2, 2026. (Photo by Ross Harried/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The Green Bay Packers had about a two-hour practice on Monday that got a chippy at the end. The first fight started between receiver Matthew Golden and edge defender Barryn Sorrell, two Texas Longhorns who were brought to the Packers via last year’s draft. According to reports from the press, linebacker Zaire Franklin and edge defender Lukas Van Ness swung in the scuffle, too. Then, receiver Will Sheppard and safety Trey Dean III, who was sent off the sideline after this dispute, got into it at the end of practice. After Monday’s fireworks, Sorrell, who is close with Golden, joked, “ It’s definitely getting time to hit somebody else .” Here’s the good news for the Packers: Today’s practice was the final open practice the team will have against each other all training camp. Green Bay’s final practice of camp will be on Wednesday, which will be a joint practice against the Arizona Cardinals. Happy JLove, LaFleur and Melton week to all who celebrate 🤝 @packers — Arizona Cardinals (@AZCardinals) August 24, 2026 Here’s what you missed at practice today, besides the fights. Injuries Green Bay’s PUP list remains unchanged, with tight end Luke Musgrave (neck), defensive lineman Jordon Riley (ankle), edge defender Micah Parsons (knee) and long snapper Matt Orzech (calf) remaining out of action. Before practice, head coach Matt LaFleur pumped the brakes on Orzech absolutely returning to practice this week, which was hinted at by general manager Brian Gutekunst last week. Yes, cornerback Brandon Cisse (knee) did return to practice today after suffering a knee injury in Week 2 of the preseason . The only players who missed practice today were receiver Savion Williams (ankle), tight end Thomas Yassmin (knee), defensive lineman Warren Brinson (calf), edge rusher Collin Oliver (calf), edge defender Arron Mosby (undisclosed), cornerback Benjamin St-Juste (hamstring) and safety Javon Bullard (foot). All of these injuries occured during Friday’s game, other than Bullard’s bone bruise. As far as we know , none of them are long-term injuries. Offense Starters: Love Jacobs – Brooks Kraft Golden – Watson Morgan – Banks – Rhyan – Monk – ZBB LVN – Brooks – Ford – Wyatt – Cooper Zaire Nixon – Hadden – Cisse Williams – X — Andy Herman (@AndyHermanNFL) August 24, 2026 The biggest question on the offensive depth chart for the Packers at this point in camp is who the starting guards will be in Week 1. In the preseason, it’s consistently been Jager Burton and Jacob Monk at the position, but neither Aaron Banks nor Zach Bako-Bewele have been thrown in when the bullets are live, and Anthony Belton, who has been Bako-Bewele’s replacement, is still involved in the right guard battle, according to Green Bay’s offensive coaches. Today, the starters were Banks at left guard (who rotated with Burton) and Monk at right guard. Belton continued to rotate at right tackle with Bako-Bewele. Both Banks and Bako-Bewele are coming off knee injuries that are limiting their full participation in practice. With the 2s Tyrod Taylor works the 2s into fg range for the tie. Smack drills a long fg to tie it up. Carrington Valentine dropped a pick on the drive. — Andy Herman (@AndyHermanNFL) August 24, 2026 Oladapo skies for a pick vs McCord. His best play of camp for sure. If today is any indication, just based on reps, McCord is of no threat at all to Tyrod. — Andy Herman (@AndyHermanNFL) August 24, 2026 While Kyle McCord has clearly put up better numbers in the preseason than Tyrod Taylor , it hasn’t been clear in practice that McCord is significantly better than Taylor as a backup option going into the 2026 season. Both quarterbacks threw bad balls in team periods today. We should get an extended look at both in the preseason finale, as LaFleur stated previously that the plan is to use the joint practice against Arizona to load up on reps for the first-team units and use the preseason game for the backups and reserves. Defense As far as the defensive lineup goes, Karl Brooks continues to get starts at 3-4 defensive end with Javon Hargrave still being a less than full particpant in practice. At the true nose, Jonathan Ford, who is competing with Nazir Stackhouse and Anthony Campbell, is getting starts regularly (he made back to back starts in the preseason), Keisean Nixon and Brandon Cisse remain the “starting” outside cornerbacks and Kamal Hadden is holding down the fort in the slot with Javon Bullard sidelined. For what it’s worth, Carrington Valentine and Domani Jackson worked with the second-team defense at cornerback today. This is notable because Valentine was generally ahead of Cisse in the cornerback pecking order this summer, when both players were healthy. These two have been competing for the right cornerback job opposite Nixon. Jackson was also behind Jaylin Simpson in the pecking order in the preseason game last week, the rookie’s debut, and might be moving up the depth chart going into his second week of camp action. Nixon seemed to have a big day today, as he had an interception of Jordan Love in a two-minute drill and also had a big pass breakup earlier in practice. Undrafted rookie Anthony Campbell continues to impressed. Just beat Travis Glover on three straight reps 1v1. Two speed rushes sandwiching a power rush where he showed great hand usage, shedding Glover. Campbell is becoming increasingly tough to cut. — Ryan Wood (@ByRyanWood) August 24, 2026 Not to be forgotten, despite Ford’s “starts” in practice is Campbell, who is still getting action against first-team offensive linemen as the defensive line rotates frequently. Campbell looked good in one-on-ones today, and continues to build buzz as a pass-rushing threat. Special Teams Rookie kicker Trey Smack hit a 60-yard field goal in a two-minute drill today and went three of four overall.

title: Packers’ Matt LaFleur gives injury updates on Brandon Cisse, Aaron Banks, others
summary: Green Bay Packers fans can breathe a sigh of relief on the statuses of a few of the team’s key players who were injured in or before Friday’s preseason game in Denver. Speaking to the press ahead of the team’s penultimate open practice on Monday, head coach Matt LaFleur provided a positive update on Brandon […]
full_text: ASHWAUBENON, WISCONSIN - JULY 31: Brandon Cisse #2 of the Green Bay Packers looks on during the Green Bay Packers training camp at Ray Nitschke Field on July 31, 2026 in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Green Bay Packers fans can breathe a sigh of relief on the statuses of a few of the team’s key players who were injured in or before Friday’s preseason game in Denver. Speaking to the press ahead of the team’s penultimate open practice on Monday, head coach Matt LaFleur provided a positive update on Brandon Cisse, while addressing the status of a few other banged-up regulars. The Packers hold an open practice at 10:30 AM Central on Monday, then will have two joint practices with the Arizona Cardinals — coached by LaFleur’s younger brother, Mike — on Wednesday and Thursday ahead of the teams’ preseason finale on Friday evening. Wednesday’s joint practice will be open to the public and will also be the final public practice of training camp. Here’s what LaFleur had to say about a few key Packers players in the Monday morning press conference. Brandon Cisse The Packers’ rookie cornerback has been working with the starting defense throughout training camp, but he got banged up covering a kickoff in Denver and did not return to the game. Thankfully, it appears that he will not miss any time and will be full-go for Monday’s practice. Cisse himself said that the injury was “nothing serious” after the game, and now LaFleur has confirmed that he will not miss any time. LaFleur: “He should be fine. He should be good to go.” Josh Jacobs The Packers have been working Jacobs into the offense gradually as he works his way back from a groin injury. Jacobs has been out of practice for almost two weeks until returning late last week. It appears that the team is continuing to be cautious with him, but he will keep ramping up over the course of this week, starting with a limited workload on Monday. LaFleur: “He’ll be limited in all team periods but he’ll be out there practicing.” When asked if Jacobs would participate in team drills, the coach responded “Oh yeah.” Aaron Banks The Packers’ assumed starting left guard has been in and out of the lineup during practices all summer with knee tendinitis, and he appeared to drop out of practice again last week. Jager Burton has been the next man up at that position when Banks has been out of the lineup, while also working in at center and right guard. However, it seems that the Packers are trying to be careful in managing Banks’ workload with the plan being to have him ready for the regular season opener. LaFleur: “He should be out there (on Monday).” When asked if Banks would be ready to be in the starting lineup for week one, LaFleur was optimistic: “I think so, I believe so. I think he’s made good progress and ultimately he’s got to continue to put those days back to back to back. He’s definitely getting better, he’s trending in the right direction.” Warren Brinson Brinson was a surprise scratch from the lineup in Friday’s game, which likely caused the coaching staff to scramble a bit to fill his snaps on the defensive line. Now is an unfortunate time for him to be out of the lineup, with the team’s other depth defensive linemen flashing, but it does appear that he will be off the field for a bit, which could affect the Packers’ decisions at final cuts on Sunday. LaFleur: “It happened in warmups, he felt a little tweak in his calf and so he’ll miss a little bit of time.” Matt Orzech Finally, the Packers’ long snapper went on the PUP list at the start of training camp and is still yet to return. Since then, Cal Adomitis has been handling those duties admirably, contributing to Trey Smack’s perfect start on place-kicks in the first two preseason games. It does seem that the Packers still like Orzech, but they must be preparing to start the season with Adomitis in that role, because it appears Orzech may not be ready to go before final cuts. LaFleur: “I think he’s getting closer. To say that he’ll be back this week might be too soon to say, but I know he’s getting close.”
author: Evan "Tex" Western

title: Has Packers’ defensive line goes from weakness to strength in record time?
summary: At the end of the 2025 season, the Green Bay Packers’ defensive line was running on fumes and waiver claims, and the team’s inability to stop the run was painfully apparent. A defense that had allowed an average of 98.3 rushing yards per game through its first 11 games gave up 164.2 yards per game […]
full_text: Chris McClellan #55 of the Green Bay Packers rides a bicycle while pointing toward the crowd during the Green Bay Packers Training Camp at Ray Nitschke Field in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin, on August 2, 2026. (Photo by Ross Harried/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images At the end of the 2025 season, the Green Bay Packers’ defensive line was running on fumes and waiver claims, and the team’s inability to stop the run was painfully apparent. A defense that had allowed an average of 98.3 rushing yards per game through its first 11 games gave up 164.2 yards per game in the final six weeks of the regular season, largely due to injuries sapping the team’s personnel. Indeed, a two-deep group of defensive tackles that included Kenny Clark, Devonte Wyatt, Karl Brooks, and Colby Wooden was left with only Brooks and Wooden at the end of the season. Clark departed for Dallas in the trade for Micah Parsons before week one, while Wyatt broke his ankle in week 13 and was out for the remainder of the season. The numbers before and after Wyatt’s injury, as shown above, illustrate how important he was to the team’s defensive line rotation and its ability to stop the run. By the end of the season, Green Bay was relying on waiver claims, practice squad pickups, and lightly-regarded rookies just to get bodies on the field. Jordon Riley, a former New York Giants practice squadder, appeared in 64 snaps over four late-season games. The Packers picked up former draft pick Jonathan Ford on waivers from the Bears and he tallied 18 snaps in the Wild Card game against his former team. Nazir Stackhouse, who made the 53 as an undrafted rookie, struggled so badly that he couldn’t even get back on the active gameday roster late in the season. Even something called a “Quinton Bohanna” made an appearance. Suddenly, however, the Packers’ interior line looks deep and exciting heading into the 2026 regular season. New additions Javon Hargrave (free agent) and Chris McClellan (3rd-round draft pick) look to provide some juice on the nose, both as run-stoppers and pocket-collapsers. Ford, whose return came very late last season, has been making plays in the preseason as a gap-filling nose tackle. Even Anthony Campbell, who signed to the practice squad before the Wild Card game, has been flashing this summer, though the Packers will be hard-pressed to keep him on the 53 since he generally does not line up at nose. Meanwhile, the returning starters all look to benefit from another offseason and a deeper rotation. Wyatt returns fully healthy and although Wooden was dealt to Indianapolis for linebacker Zaire Franklin, he was miscast as a nose tackle anyway. Brooks looks set for a starting role, but this deeper group should allow him to stay well south of the 40-plus snaps per game that he averaged in 2025 (he averaged just 26 snaps per game in his much better 2024). Warren Brinson, a 6th-round pick in 2025, has shown signs of improvement during the summer, though he did miss the second preseason game with an injury. Although the Packers are returning to a 3-4 base defense in name, this team will be in nickel almost all the time, which means there will be two interior linemen on the field on most snaps. And on passing downs, edge rushers like Lukas Van Ness, Barryn Sorrell, and Dani Dennis-Sutton are all candidates to shift inside and pin their ears back. Perhaps the biggest pivot point on this year’s line will be McClellan. If the rookie can quickly earn significant snaps at the nose and hold up well against the run, everything else should fall into place. Wyatt and Brooks are at their best when they can rotate at the 3-tech, while Hargrave should provide veteran insurance across the entire interior. Brinson and Ford seem best positioned to round out the group, with the former also able to play all across the front and Ford a candidate to get a few snaps per game in obvious running situations. Depth, more than anything, should help the Packers’ defensive line function better in 2026 than it did in 2025. They should be better able to withstand the inevitable bumps and bruises that take place across a rigorous schedule, and hopefully a few useful players can make it through waivers onto the practice squad to provide additional insurance. If the Packers’ run defense improves drastically in 2026 from the level of play it displayed late in 2025, it should come as little surprise. Look for an uptick in the quality of the team’s interior pass rush as well, which will be critical early in the season as the team awaits the return of Micah Parsons on the edge.

title: Packers Film Room, Preseason Week 2: Trey Smack
summary: By now, I think we’ve all seen Green Bay Packers special teams coordinator Cam Achord’s presser where he talked about how the hold will change depending on different factors while kicking a field goal. But, in case you missed it, here it is: Here’s a bit of a summary:1. A lot of kickers like the […]
full_text: By now, I think we’ve all seen Green Bay Packers special teams coordinator Cam Achord’s presser where he talked about how the hold will change depending on different factors while kicking a field goal. But, in case you missed it, here it is: First-year Packers special teams coordinator Cam Achord was asked how Trey Smack likes his kicks to be held. He then came off the podium and did this for almost two minutes. Enjoy. pic.twitter.com/sD6yhBbZDB — Matt Schneidman (@mattschneidman) August 5, 2026 Here’s a bit of a summary: 1. A lot of kickers like the ball straight up and down. 2. If you want to drive the ball through the wind, lean the ball forward a bit. “Most guys who kick in weather have a forward lean.” 3. The direction of the wind can inform the direction of the horizontal lean. 4. Some kickers like a more extreme horizontal angle. 5. By adjusting the football, the kicker doesn’t have to change his swing. The lean of the ball can help do some of the work for him. So, basically, the amount of lean will change depending on the kicker and the elements. Knowing that Trey Smack is the kicker – and will be the kicker heading into the regular season – let’s look at his field goal kicks against the Broncos. I took his four field goal attempts (all makes, of course) and slowed down the snap-to-kick portion. Field Goal 1: 50 Yards The flags on the uprights are pretty still. I see forward lean on the hold, without much of a horizontal lean in either direction. Maybe a slight lean away from Smack. Field Goal 2: 59 yards You can’t see the uprights in this clip, but this is a forward lean away from Smack. Big fan of his celebration after it goes through. Field Goal 3: 43 yards The flags are pushing ever-so-slightly to the left of the screen. The hold is a forward lean with a slight lean away from Smack (with the wind). Field Goal 4: 38 yards Flags are dead. Not much wind in Denver, apparently. This appears to be a forward lean away from Smack. With all that in mind, it looks like Smack’s preference is likely a slight forward lean, with a horizontal lean slightly away from him. While this game is outside, the conditions appear to be ideal: very little wind, no precipitation, with an added boost of being in the thin Denver air. I think it’s fair to assume that this is how he wants the ball held in ideal conditions. I’m curious to see how this changes if there’s wind and/or precipitation. Albums listened to: Jessica Lea Mayfield – Miss Obliteration

title: Houston Texans Wide Receiver Room Update
summary: The Houston Texans took a massive hit at wide receiver last week when promising second-year wide receiver Jayden Higgins suffered a season-ending torn ACL. General manager Nick Caserio responded quickly, adding veteran wide receivers Zay Jones and Sterling Shepard. While both additions provided much-needed depth at training camp, it still felt like Houston needed another […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 22: Kayshon Boutte #9 of the New England Patriots runs against the Philadelphia Eagles prior to an NFL preseason football game at Gillette Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Houston Texans took a massive hit at wide receiver last week when promising second-year wide receiver Jayden Higgins suffered a season-ending torn ACL. General manager Nick Caserio responded quickly, adding veteran wide receivers Zay Jones and Sterling Shepard. While both additions provided much-needed depth at training camp, it still felt like Houston needed another legitimate weapon to stabilize the position heading into the 2026 season. The Texans began calling around the league and gauging the asking prices for several wide receivers before ultimately pulling the trigger Monday, acquiring Kayshon Boutte from the New England Patriots. Houston sent safety Jaylen Reed and a 2028 seventh-round pick to New England in exchange for the 24-year-old receiver. Boutte became one of Drake Maye’s most dangerous downfield weapons in New England. Last season, he finished with 33 receptions for 551 yards and six touchdowns while averaging 16.7 yards per reception. He also played a role in the Patriots’ run to the Super Bowl, including a touchdown against Houston in the Divisional Round. Now, the former LSU standout gets an opportunity to step into a significant role in Houston during the final year of his rookie contract. A strong 2026 season could also put Boutte in position to cash in when he becomes a free agent next offseason. More importantly, he gives the Texans something they desperately need. Houston’s offense was far too one-dimensional last season and consistently struggled to create explosive plays. Higgins was expected to take another step forward and help change that in 2026, making his season-ending injury such a significant loss. Boutte isn’t a one-for-one replacement for Higgins, but his ability to stretch the field gives C.J. Stroud another legitimate weapon and adds a different dimension to the offense. Everyone knows Houston’s defense is good enough to carry this team deep into the season. But if the Texans want to finally break through and make a legitimate Super Bowl run, they need more from their offense. Adding Boutte gives them another opportunity to find it. Here is a look at the notable wide receivers currently on Houston’s roster: Nico Collins Kayshon Boutte Tank Dell Jaylin Noel Xavier Hutchinson Lewis Bond Sterling Shepard Zay Jones There are still plenty of questions surrounding the group, especially when it comes to health and availability. Dell is working his way back from a significant knee injury, while Noel has also dealt with injuries during training camp. But if Houston can get this group healthy and keep it that way, there is plenty of talent for Stroud to work with. Losing Higgins was a massive blow. Adding Boutte doesn’t completely erase it, but it gives the Texans another explosive weapon — and some much-needed hope that this offense can reach another level in 2026.

title: TRADE! Texans trade for Patriots WR Kayshon Boutte
summary: There is a term in Texas no-limit hold’em poker when you bet all the money you have on your hand in a single bet. Most people know it, but for the uninitiated, it’s called going “all in.” Going all in can be a sign of desperation, such as when a player has very little money […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - AUGUST 22: Kayshon Boutte #9 of the New England Patriots in warm up before a preseason game between the New England Patriots and the Philadelphia Eagles on August 22, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images There is a term in Texas no-limit hold’em poker when you bet all the money you have on your hand in a single bet. Most people know it, but for the uninitiated, it’s called going “all in.” Going all in can be a sign of desperation, such as when a player has very little money and is trying to survive another round of betting; but it can also be a sign of supreme confidence. This is the move one makes when they know, with mathematical certainty, that they have the best possible hand. In this situation, it’s a power move. This is the Houston Texans going all in. This is their power move. The Texans lost their WR2 Jayden Higgins for the season due to a torn ACL at practice. But rather than standing pat and going with the receivers they have, they decided to bolster the WR corps with an up-and coming prospect for the remainder of the year. Trade! The Patriots are sending WR Kayshon Boutte to the Texans for safety Jaylen Reed and a draft pick, sources tell @ringer @netflixsports . pic.twitter.com/NZXCdOX4RT — Tom Pelissero (@TomPelissero) August 24, 2026 The New England Patriots, by all accounts, really liked Boutte and had asked for a high price even for a one year rental, which Boutte almost assuredly would be. He had recently become one of Drake Maye’s favorite targets. Now he can work as a WR2 in an offense that promises to share a lot of yardage. To quote Pats Pulpit about Kayshon Boutte: Boutte, 24, originally joined the Patriots as a sixth-round pick in 2023 out of LSU. Following a quiet rookie season with the team that saw him mostly serve as a healthy scratch, he showed some significant progress the next two seasons and developed in one of quarterback Drake Maye’s favorite receivers. In total, he ends his Patriots career having appeared in a combined 38 regular season and playoff games. Along the way, he caught 87 passes for 1,327 yards — an average of 15.3 yards per catch — and 10 touchdowns. Despite his growth and role in the offense, Boutte had been the subject of trade rumors for two straight offseasons. No trade materialized in 2025, but the circumstances changed in 2026 following the Patriots’ acquisitions of fellow wide receivers A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs. Boutte requested a trade in the spring, and now has gotten his wish. This feels like a pretty fair deal to me. The Patriots get a good defensive player and some draft capital. The Texans get a potential WR2 who can complement Nico Collins and spell the rest of the WR corps. Kayshon Boutte gets his wish of leaving New England and a chance to prove he’s worth his next contract. The Texans go all in and everyone wins, this time hopefully including the Lombardi.

title: Five Texans Appear on NFL Top 100
summary: Over the course of last week, the NFL revealed #20-11 on the NFL’s Top 100 Players of 2026 rankings. If you haven’t heard of it before, this list is a ranking of the “best 100 players currently in the NFL as voted on by active players,” and is yet another accolade for these tenaciously talented […]
full_text: Over the course of last week, the NFL revealed #20-11 on the NFL’s Top 100 Players of 2026 rankings. If you haven’t heard of it before, this list is a ranking of the “best 100 players currently in the NFL as voted on by active players,” and is yet another accolade for these tenaciously talented athletes to covet. All players respect a vote of confidence from their peers, and Houston’s uber-talented roster has received some of the most attention of all teams. Last Friday, the NFL revealed the final spots before the top 10, and Texans DE Will Anderson Jr. was #12 on the list! No. 12 on the NFL Top 100 Players of 2026… @HoustonTexans DE Will Anderson Jr.! @NFLFilms pic.twitter.com/GLV6VZOLlH — NFL (@NFL) August 21, 2026 Anderson, who will turn 25 on on September 2nd and is entering fourth NFL season, has already earned admiration from the vast majority of his peers. Indianapolis Colts TE Mo Alie-Cox despairs at Anderson’s get-off speed as the ball is snapped, and Seahawks guard Grey Label goes as far to say, “I think he’s starting to enter the conversation of, like, a top three, top five pass rusher in the NFL right now.” I guess when you make a weekly habit of flying around blockers like a rogue boomerang and averaging 10.0 sacks a year, people start to notice! Anderson’s final stats of the 2026 season were: 19 Games (19 Starts – Incl. Playoffs) 54 Combined Tackles 17.0 Sacks, 24 QB Hits, 102 Total Pressures (Incl. Playoffs) 3 Pass Deflections, 6 Forced Fumbles (Incl. Playoffs), 2 Fumble Recoveries, 1 Fumble Recovered for a Touchdown 779 Total Snaps, 93.4 OFF Grade (78.6 RDEF, 51.5 TACK, 92.8 PRSH, 76.9 COV) Pro-Bowl, First Team All-Pro This marks, in all likelihood, the last Texan on the NFL Top 100 players of 2026 list. Anderson’s 12th-place finish is the highest a Houston Texans player has landed on this list since 2019, when WR DeAndre Hopkins ranked 11th following his 1,572-yard. 11-touchdown campaign in 2018. Anderson actually tied DE J.J. Watt at 12th on this same list (both in 2019 and in 2014 ), making Anderson the highest ranked Texans defender since Watt was ranked 3rd in 2016. It’s still early in his career, but Will Anderson is already surrounding himself with very, very good company. Anderson is also the fifth Texans player to be named in this Top 100, tying a franchise record of Texans on the list that was made last year. The full list this year includes: LB Azeez Al- Shaair ( #92 – Was Unranked Last Year) WR Nico Collins ( #58 – Was #32 Last Year) CB Derek Stingley, Jr. ( #25 – Was #18 Last Year) DE Danielle Hunter ( #23 – Was #25 Last Year) DE Will Anderson, Jr. ( #12 – Was #46 Last Year) Note: LB Azeez Al-Shaair is making his first appearance in the Top 100 this year, and QB C.J. Stroud has fallen off the list since last year. Click here to see Houston’s 2025 Rankings Click here to see Houston’s 2024 Rankings All three levels of Houston’s swarming defense are represented on the top 100. Many things are difficult when it comes to being a Texans fan, but at this moment in time, we can take solace in bearing witness to one of the most complete defensive rosters to ever grace a professional football field. Rarely has a group of players so talented, aggressive, smart, and instinctive ever been brought under the same roof to represent one franchise, and it may be years until we ever see something like this again. This Top 100 group represents Houston’s sheer dominance on defense, but it also reflects the lopsided view many hold of the Texans team as of late. WR Nico Collins is the only offensive player on this list, and QB C.J. Stroud has fallen entirely off the Top 100 after being ranked in each of his first two years. Not the trajectory you want your franchise signal-caller to be going, but it’s worth bearing in mind that this is not a “definitive” ranking of players in the NFL. There are pro-bowl, superstar caliber players that miss the Top 100 all the time, and even though Stroud was certainly not either one of those things in 2025, his year was at least comparable to what it was in 2024, if not better. What I believe knocked him off this season’s rankings were his performances in the playoffs against the Pittsburgh Steelers and New England Patriots. Those were arguably his worst two games in his NFL career, and it’ll be hard to wipe those off his record for a long while. Unfortunately, no Texans players made the top ten this year, so we have seen the last Houston player to make the Top 100. But, there’s still multiple Texans players that I think deserved to appear somewhere on this list, even if they don’t carry the reputation others do. The best Texans players to be snubbed a Top 100 spot are: CB Kamari Lassiter S Jalen Pitre S Calen Bullock RG Ed Ingram QB C.J. Stroud For the #Texans , I count for sure seven: – Al-Shaair (Top 100) – Bullock (Top 100) – Lassiter (Top 70) – Collins (Top 50) – Stingley (Top 40) – Hunter (Top 40) – Anderson (Fringe Top 10) Stroud probably will get consideration. Montgomery (via Lions) might make it. https://t.co/QIWQN1vP4p — Cole Thompson (@MrColeThompson) June 26, 2026 Bullock and Ingram missing the ranking is understandable, but I’ve been scratching my head as to how Pitre nor Lassiter missed the cutoff for the last several days. You could argue that Kamari Lassiter had just as good of a season in 2025 as his 25th-ranked counterpart in Derek Stingley, Jr., yet he didn’t even crack the list. Jalen Pitre has virtually personified the phrase, “hard-hitting defender” and has succeeded in making the NFL’s Guardian Cap appear more like a weapon than a piece of protective headgear, and yet, he couldn’t even get enough votes to pass up Saints DE Cameron Jordan? Sounds pretty suspect to me, but hey, they’re the players, and they can vote on themselves however they see fit. What do you think of where these Texans players landed on the Top 100? Should Will Anderson or some other players been ranked higher? Should C.J. Stroud have appeared on the list? Are there any other Texans that should have landed in the Top 100, like Pitre or Lassiter? Let us know your thoughts on the rankings down in the comments below! Go Texans!

title: Colts look in preseason form.
summary: There is not much sugar coating the Atlanta game, but it is not as bad when you are not expecting mid-season form. I saw a couple of things that can’t make their way to regular season, but I saw a lot of searching for answers as well. From most reports, we used mostly second stringers […]
full_text: There is not much sugar coating the Atlanta game, but it is not as bad when you are not expecting mid-season form. I saw a couple of things that can’t make their way to regular season, but I saw a lot of searching for answers as well. From most reports, we used mostly second stringers against Atlanta’s second stringers. Once the regular season starts, all we need is for individual second stringers to fill in well for a starter, not to win our 2nd 22 versus other team’s 2nd 22s. No news here, but with a roster of around 90 that has to be finalized at 53, along with your 16 Practice Squad players, we will cut 20 or so players. One note, PS squads must contain at least 10 1st year players or rookies, but can have up to six players with unlimited experience. Much is made about who is placed on the practice squad and how tenuous their ability to stay there would be. One thing to remember is that a team can’t poach one of your PS players to their own PS. If they select one of your players, they have to be placed on their 53 man roster. So the preseason is mostly about who gets cut. I think that I saw some questions trying to be answered. Did anyone notice that most of the first half saw an interior line of LG Tucker, C Kreutz, and RB Morrissey? I think Tucker was just out there for some LG run to add to his RG and Center work, while Morrissey got time at guard to check his ability beyond backup Center. I think Kreutz found his way to the cut line, but I’m not trying to say who makes the team or not. I am saying that I think they are trying to figure out which nine OL should make the 53, based on providing the best backup at five positions. I also think that Ajiake was being given an audition to begin the season as a starter, with the green dot. He started and played quite a bit with that designation and had pretty good game. Allen also wore the dot when he got his snaps. The fact that Allen played means two things. One, he hasn’t practiced enough as a rookie and secondly, he hasn’t secured the starting position that most expected him to fill immediately. That adds to why I believe Ajiake is being given that opportunity. The defense wasn’t good as a whole, so maybe he didn’t do the green dot job so well? One thing that I am noticing is that our DEs are putting a hand in the dirt less often. It let’s them move a little more, prior to the snap, in an attempt to find the best rushing angle. It also allows them to drop in coverage, which is a tactic that Lou likes, as evidenced by Latu’s three interceptions last year. When trying to sort out what sort of rotation we might see, or even who makes the final 53 man roster, paying attention to who looks best in coverage, might be the tie-breaker. Curry and Gumbs look the part, but that could be because of jersey numbers in the 50s, more than anything tangible that I have witnessed. We will obviously give JT the ball often, but I am now worrying about depth. McGowan may be all we need back there, but the availability of others has me wondering if a bargain vet may be necessary? Another worry is that many see both Blackmon and Edwards making the team. I still think Jones and Carter might be the better way to go, as even second string QBs are playing “Where’s Waldo”, when targeting our defenders. One other slight concern is that we didn’t bring in a camp body to spell Rigo. I know that you can pick up punters off of the street, but I also know that we lost him for a year once, so it might not have been a bad idea to have had a guy in camp that you kept on speed dial. I guess it wouldn’t be a Colts piece, if I didn’t mention the QBs. To start with, if we lose our starter, our chances at competing are greatly diminished. Maybe both would look amazing with the starters, but I do not see either of them looking as good as Jones looked piloting the ship last year. My hope is that any drama associated with the status of our QB2, is limited to depth charts and game day designations. I still wont be shocked if we get a call from a team that loses their QB1 and finally makes an offer for Richardson that Ballard would accept. All in all, I’m just like everyone else who is waiting to see if we get starters for a quarter against the Lions, or at least a couple of drives? I feel better about the depth than you would expect after the kind of beating we took against the Falcons, but as an optimist, that shouldn’t be unexpected. So, the question this week is, “Did our performance against Atlanta change your perception of the Colts as we approach opening day?

title: Spencer Shrader or Blake Grupe?
summary: I’ve played golf religiously my whole life and when things are tough, I try to always bring it back to something I know and that’s usually golf. The Spencer Shrader vs Blake Grupe battle is very close and is essentially a coinflip to decide who will win the battle. But to me, there’s one thing […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, IN - AUGUST 20: Indianapolis Colts kicker Spencer Shrader (3) runs through a drill during the Indianapolis Colts and Atlanta Falcons joint training camp practice on August 20, 2026 at the Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images I’ve played golf religiously my whole life and when things are tough, I try to always bring it back to something I know and that’s usually golf. The Spencer Shrader vs Blake Grupe battle is very close and is essentially a coinflip to decide who will win the battle. But to me, there’s one thing that separates the two. In golf, many guys are great on the range. They stripe the ball and they look like PGA Tour pros out there. Their swing is effortless, the ball flies and it lands on a dime. They can do this over and over again. Then they get to the course, and suddenly the swing tightens up. That effortless motion becomes choppier, the ball starts slicing or hooking, and the player who looked automatic on the range looks completely different when the shot actually counts. The point is simple: some players are just different when the pressure is turned up and the lights get bright. Colts ST coordinator Brian Mason is going to have a tough decision. *Spencer Shrader 32/46 (69.6 pct) in camp; 4/4 in 2 preseason games. *Blake Grupe 41/45 (91.1 pct) in camp, 0/2 in 2 preseason games. My gut tells me they're keeping Shrader. — Mike Chappell (@mchappell51) August 22, 2026 That is how I look at this Colts kicking battle right now. Blake Grupe has had the better training camp. By the reported numbers, he has made over 90 percent of his kicks, while Shrader has been under 70 percent. In most position battles, that kind of camp gap would be hard to ignore. Practice matters, consistency matters, and Grupe deserves credit for stacking good days in a setting where coaches are evaluating every rep. The problem is that kicker is not like most positions, and this battle has looked very different once the Colts have gotten into games. Shrader has gone 4-for-4 in the preseason, including makes from 61 and 53 yards. Grupe, meanwhile, is 0-for-2 in game action so far. That does not erase his strong camp, and it does not make Shrader’s camp struggles irrelevant, but it changes the weight of the conversation. Practice tells you who can make kicks in a controlled environment. Games tell you who can make kicks when the operation, rush, timing and pressure all feel closer to what the job actually is. Kicking and hitting a golf ball are actually quite similar in many ways. Many kickers like to play a draw on the ball, while others like to play a cut. The plant step is crucially important because it sets up the swing of the kicking leg properly. Ideally for kickers, the ball is struck around the middle of the swing of the kicking leg. If a right-footed kicker plants too far in front of the ball, the ball can be blocked and flare out right. If he plants too far behind the ball, he catches it later in the swing and the ball can be pulled left. The swing of the leg works on an arc, almost like a half-moon, and when the timing is clean, everything looks easy. That is why practice can be misleading with kickers. When you are on the range or taking camp kicks, you can find rhythm and repeat the motion because the setting is controlled. There is no real consequence, no full game pressure, no rush affecting your mind, and no threat of the moment swallowing the technique. It is much easier to focus on the perfect plant step when nothing is closing in on you and the kick does not actually decide anything. In games, that changes fast. The operation has to be clean, the timing has to hold up, defenders are coming, and the pressure of the moment can pull your mind away from the small details that make the kick work. On a long field goal especially, the slightest change can make all the difference. Plant a little too far in front, and the ball can flare right. Plant a little too far behind, and it can start left. The best kickers are the ones who can keep the same rhythm, same plant, same swing and same focus when the kick actually matters. Many guys can do it in practice and far fewer can do it when the lights are on. That is why Shrader’s preseason is so important! He has not just made kicks; he has made big kicks. A 61-yarder and a 53-yarder in game settings are not small data points. Those are exactly the types of kicks that tell a coaching staff something about a player’s mind, not just his leg. Shrader has shown that even if his camp has been uneven, he can walk into a game setting and deliver when the rep feels closer/closest to the real thing. Grupe was great for the Colts last season, and that should not be dismissed. He came in and gave the team good kicking, and his overall resume in Indianapolis is part of the reason this competition is so close. At the same time, kicker is probably the biggest “what have you done for me lately?” position in football. Teams can love your past production, but if the current competition is happening right now, the current kicks have to carry more weight. Last year should matter, but it should be weighted less than what the Colts are seeing in games this summer. That is where I land on this battle. Grupe has been better in camp, and if this were only about practice numbers, he would have the edge. Once the preseason games are included, Shrader should be ahead. He has been better when the lights are on, and for kickers, that matters more than almost anything else. This does not mean Grupe is bad, and it does not mean the decision is easy. The Colts would probably love to keep both in the building if they can, because each kicker has made a legitimate case in a different way. Grupe has shown the steadier camp leg, while Shrader has shown the better game leg. The problem is that only one can realistically be the kicker, and if the question is who should be trusted when the kick actually matters, Shrader has given the better answer so far. Unless something changes before the final decision, Shrader should be ahead, and he should probably be the one the Colts keep.

title: Chiefs sign defensive end Niles King, waive injured rookie Jeff Caldwell
summary: On Monday afternoon, the Kansas City Chiefs added another player to the defensive line room after signing veteran Emmanuel Ogbah just a few weeks ago. Defensive end Niles King is a rookie from San Diego State who was initially signed by the Los Angeles Chargers this spring after going undrafted in the 2026 NFL Draft. […]
full_text: SAN DIEGO, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 22: Niles King #44 of the San Diego State Aztecs works against Tyler Chen #62 of the San Jose State Spartans during the second half at Snapdragon Stadium on November 22, 2025 in San Diego, California. (Photo by Orlando Ramirez/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Monday afternoon, the Kansas City Chiefs added another player to the defensive line room after signing veteran Emmanuel Ogbah just a few weeks ago. We have signed Free Agent DE Niles King. We have waived WR Jeff Caldwell with an injury designation. pic.twitter.com/bMtWi74p9B — Kansas City Chiefs (@Chiefs) August 24, 2026 Defensive end Niles King is a rookie from San Diego State who was initially signed by the Los Angeles Chargers this spring after going undrafted in the 2026 NFL Draft. King was let go just weeks after signing with the Chiefs’ AFC West rival. With the Aztecs for just one season, King totaled 6.5 sacks, 10 tackles for loss and 30 combined tackles during the 2025 campaign. He ranked seventh in the Mountain West Conference in sacks and tackles for loss. Prior to San Diego State, King played four seasons at Grand Valley State University. At his Pro Day, King measured nearly 6 feet 6 inches tall and 265 pounds; his arm length was 34 5/8 inches, and his hands measured 10 1/8 inches. King’s arm length is now the longest among the Chiefs’ defensive ends on the 90-man roster. To make room for the defensive end, the Chiefs waived rookie wide receiver Jeff Caldwell with an injury designation. If Caldwell clears waivers, he could be assigned to the Reserve/Injured list for the 2026 season.

title: Andy Reid gives Chiefs injury update, Trey Smith back at practice
summary: After the Kansas City Chiefs’ 16-15 defeat at the hands of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in NFL preseason Week 2, the team is back at practice — but not in St. Joseph, Missouri. Training camp concluded last week, so the Chiefs are settling back into the team facilities at One Arrowhead Drive. Head coach Andy […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - AUGUST 15: Guard Trey Smith #65 of the Kansas City Chiefs listens to teammates on the sidelines during fourth quarter game action in an NFL preseason game against the Los Angeles Rams at Arrowhead Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images After the Kansas City Chiefs ’ 16-15 defeat at the hands of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in NFL preseason Week 2, the team is back at practice — but not in St. Joseph, Missouri. Training camp concluded last week, so the Chiefs are settling back into the team facilities at One Arrowhead Drive. Head coach Andy Reid stepped up to the podium before Monday’s practice to update the local media on the players currently injured. Players who will not practice on Monday Wide receiver Jeff Caldwell (Hyperextended Knee) Linebacker Jack Cochrane (Knee) Safety Chamarri Conner Defensive end Ashton Gillotte (Plantar fascia) Safety Alohi Gilman (Low-back spasms) Guard C.J. Hanson Wide reciver Jimmy Holiday Quarterback Chris Oladokun (Concussion) Left tackle Josh Simmons (Lower back) Defensive end Tyreke Smith (Hamstring) Right guard Trey Smith returns to practice Excluded from Reid’s rundown was right guard Trey Smith, who missed the majority of padded practices in training camp due to a hip injury that was significant enough for Smith to go see a hip specialist. It’s a relief to hear the team’s starting right guard is back on the practice field with a few weeks to go until Week 1. “We’ll ease him back in, but he wants to get out there and get going,” Reid described Smith. “It has been killing him not to be out there. He’s kind of wired that way.” “Trey loves to play,” Reid elaborated. “But it was important that he let that thing heal up like he did. I think it will pay off for him down the road.” Will Patrick Mahomes play in preseason Week 3? “He’s doing great; we’ll just see,” Reid responded when asked about starting quarterback Patrick Mahomes playing against the Seattle Seahawks in preseason Week 3. “If the doctors and trainers and everybody that’s involved give him the okay, and most of all, if he feels like he can, then we’ll address that when we get there.” Patrick Mahomes provides an update on his left knee: "I feel great … I really wanted to play today … I'll wait until Coach Reid lets me go, but I'm ready … I'll be trying to play next week … I'm going to be ready to go for that 1st game of the year, God willing" #Chiefs pic.twitter.com/Ca8fKniHHo — Mark Poulose (@MarkPoulose) August 23, 2026 During an in-game interview with the Chiefs’ broadcast team on Saturday, Mahomes made it clear that he’s ready to be on the field, claiming “he really wanted to play today.” “He wants to play every weekend,” Reid said when provided with Mahomes’ input. The Chiefs will begin the normal, regular-season practice routine this week before the preseason finale on Friday evening at Arrowhead Stadium.

title: Chiefs 53-man roster prediction 2.0
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs have finished training camp and played two exhibition games. The Arrowhead Pride staff has been locked into the entire preseason process, publishing a 53-man roster prediction after one week of camp. Here’s an updated prediction with just one preseason game left: Offense (26) Quarterbacks (3): Patrick Mahomes, Justin Fields and Garrett […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - AUGUST 22: Jake Briningstool #88 of the Kansas City Chiefs celebrates a first down catch against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the first half of a preseason game at Raymond James Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs have finished training camp and played two exhibition games. The Arrowhead Pride staff has been locked into the entire preseason process, publishing a 53-man roster prediction after one week of camp . Here’s an updated prediction with just one preseason game left: Offense (26) Quarterbacks (3): Patrick Mahomes, Justin Fields and Garrett Nussmeier NO CHANGE I’ve been confident in rookie Garrett Nussmeier’s ability since he performed well in camp. His preseason performances have only solidified his spot on the roster. Running backs (4): Kenneth Walker, Brashard Smith, Emari Demercado and Emmett Johnson NO CHANGE I’ll repeat the opening line from the initial update: “This group feels pretty set in stone as the team’s backfield for this season.” However, there’s reason to believe rookie Emmett Johnson is higher on the backfield totem pole than I initially believed. Each back is going to have a role on the team, but Johnson looks like the obvious choice to take the lion’s share of the reps if starter Kenneth Walker is ever unavailable. Wide receivers (6): Rashee Rice, Xavier Worthy, Tyquan Thornton, Cyrus Allen, Jalen Royals and Andrew Armstrong NO CHANGE Nikko Remigio, the team’s starting kick and punt returner currently, is looming over a group that looks better by the day. I believe it would be a mistake to cut one of these 6 players in favor of keeping Remigio, especially when Brashard Smith appears to be a quality option to return kicks. Tight ends (4): Travis Kelce, Noah Gray , Jared Wiley and Jake Briningstool CHANGE: Jake Briningstool makes the cut There’s a case to be made that the Chiefs’ reserve tight ends are not an important enough group to roster three tight ends behind the legendary Travis Kelce, who will take the bulk of the snaps this year, whether the team’s winning or losing (proved by his reliability down the stretch of last year’s lost season). However, Briningstool has made enough of a statement in training camp and the preseason to deserve a spot on an NFL 53-man roster. With the future of the tight end position in question, the young pass catcher from Clemson could be a bigger part of the offense in future seasons. Offensive linemen (9): LT Joshua Simmons, LG Kingsley Suamataia, C Creed Humphrey, RG Trey Smith, RT Jaylon Moore, Kahlil Benson, Esa Pole, Hunter Nourzad and Mike Caliendo NO CHANGE We still don’t know exactly what the starting offensive line will look like in Week 1, but I have a hard time seeing the unit shape up any other way. While the team tries to figure out if rookie Kahlil Benson can play guard, it’s worth keeping around interior backups like Nourzad and Caliendo, who have been with the team for multiple years. Defense (24) Defensive tackles (4): Chris Jones, Khyiris Tonga, Peter Woods and Marcus Harris CHANGE: Marcus Harris in place of Omarr Norman-Lott on PUP As the season draws near, the realization of second-year defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott’s recovery timeline has hit. He has been on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list for the entirety of training camp, and there’s a chance he starts the season still on the list. That would force him to miss at least the first four games of the season. If we project that to be the case, the answer for who the Chiefs’ fourth defensive tackle would be is easy: second-year player Marcus Harris from Auburn has flashed throughout camp and in the preseason, especially Week 2. Defensive ends (5): George Karlaftis, Ashton Gillotte, Felix Anudike-Uzomah, R Mason Thomas and Emmanuel Ogbah CHANGE: Emmanuel Ogbah in place of Tyreke Smith When I first started drawing up a 53-man roster prediction earlier this summer, I had “veteran defensive end” written in as the fifth player for the edge defenders. The signing of Ogbah always seemed like a natural move to make before the season begins. Linebackers (5): Nick Bolton, Drue Tranquill, Jeffrey Bassa, Cooper McDonald and Jack Cochrane NO CHANGE There’s nothing to change here, although it is interesting that veteran linebacker Cole Christiansen has been so involved in the Chiefs’ starting special teams this preseason. That might be because Cochrane is playing more with the starting defense in place of linebacker Drue Tranquill. Former Chiefs linebacker and special-teams player Cam Jones was also signed recently, but there’s only one spot for the special-teams-only reserve in this group, and Cochrane has seemingly earned it. Cornerbacks (5): Mansoor Delane, Nohl Williams, L’Jarius Sneed, Jadon Canady and Kevin Knowles CHANGES: Cut (or trade) Kristian Fulton Kevin Knowles in place of Kader Kohou There has not been any evidence that veteran Kristian Fulton has any kind of role in the Chiefs’ defense through two preseason games. He has been with the second-team defense through camp and the exhibition games, even playing behind Melvin Smith Jr. in the opening exhibition. The team would immediately save $5 million by cutting him, which is probably more likely than finding a trade partner. The Chiefs guaranteed Kohou $1.8 million this season in an attempt to find a reliable slot defender for the Chiefs’ defense. In the preseason, it appears safety Christian Roland-Wallace has manned that spot in the first-team defense, and rookie Jadon Canady has flashed as seemingly a slot-only defender so far. Kohou seems to be lost in the mix, and with Knowles’ key role in the Chiefs’ special teams, the second-year defensive back from Florida State seems to be in line to make the team over the newcoming veteran. Safeties (5): Alohi Gilman, Chamarri Conner, Christian Roland-Wallace, Jaden Hicks and Xavier Nwankpa NO CHANGE This group seems pretty straightforward, especially now that third-year safety Jaden Hicks has come on strong in preseason games, potentially strengthening the depth of the young, fresh-faced secondary in 2026. Specialists (3) Placekicker Harrison Butker, punter Matt Araiza and long snapper James Winchester The usual suspects.
