title: New York Jets defense under Aaron Glenn: When is a 3-4 defense not a 3-4 defense?
summary: The Jets’ search for a new defensive coordinator in the early stages of the offseason had plenty of twists and turns. It ended with the team hiring former Miami Dolphins passing game coordinator Brian Duker to replace Steve Wilks. Duker’s resume was a tad light for a coordinator so it surprised few after the hire […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - AUGUST 14: Head Coach Aaron Glenn of the New York Jets looks on prior to the game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at MetLife Stadium on August 14, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Evan Bernstein/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jets’ search for a new defensive coordinator in the early stages of the offseason had plenty of twists and turns. It ended with the team hiring former Miami Dolphins passing game coordinator Brian Duker to replace Steve Wilks. Duker’s resume was a tad light for a coordinator so it surprised few after the hire when head coach Aaron Glenn announced he would take on playcalling duties. At a few points over the course of the offseason Glenn suggested the team is moving to a 3-4 base defense away from the 4-3 base Wilks operated. Aaron Glenn said the Jets will play a 3-4 base defense with No. 2 overall pick David Bailey at outside linebacker. Glenn, however, has also downplayed any switch to a 3-4 defense. “You do hear that a lot, and I will say this, we are, we will be a multiple defense. So there will be elements of 4-3, there will be elements of 3-4… I don’t want to sit here and say exactly who we’re going to be, because we’re going to be a little bit of everything.” What is Glenn talking about? What do we make of this? Let’s talk a bit about the evolution of defensive systems. I’ll put out the disclaimer in advance that this article will contain some massive oversimplifications for the sake of clarity. When you study football history, you’ll find that schematic innovations tend to have a thousand fathers. There normally isn’t a single inventor of a concept. A few coaches stumble upon something new independent of each other. The new concept works well, and everybody else adopts it. Again, I state this just so you understand that I probably will be leaving out key figures involved with the rises of the schemes I’m about to mention for the sake of clarity. Most football historians have settled on crediting Tom Landry as the coach who took the 4-3 defense to the mainstream. The 4-3 contains 4 defensive linemen and 3 linebackers. (As a good rule of thumb, any defense described by a number lists the number of defensive linemen first, linebackers second, and optionally the number of players in the secondary third. One exception is Buddy Ryan’s 46 defense which was named after the jersey number of a key player, number 46 Doug Plank. We won’t discuss the 46 today.) Landry first used the defense in the 1950s as defensive coordinator of the New York Giants. One of the big drivers in this was the increase in the use of the passing game in offenses during this era. It is disputed whether the Giants were playing a 5-2 or a 6-1 prior to Landry implementing the 4-3. In any event, replacing linemen with extra linebackers provided players who were more adept in coverage against passing offenses, which were becoming more sophisticated at the time. (Another common thread through the history of professional football is that the prevalence of the passing game consistently rises. Coaches constantly figure out new and more efficient ways to stress defenses throwing the ball. The league itself also has consistently changed its rules to make throwing easier. The people running the NFL realize that fans love wide open football so they lean into it.) An example of a 4-3 defensive front can be seen below in a hi-tech GGN graphic. You might notice the way the linebackers are labeled. It is based on their spot in the formation. There is a strong side and a weak side. The strong side is the side of the field where the tight end lines up. It is strong because the tight end adds an extra body. The weak side is the other side. It is weak because there are fewer players there. The tight end is across the field after all. The SLB is the strong side linebacker. You might hear him described as the SAM linebacker. The MLB is the middle linebacker. You might hear him described as the MIKE linebacker. Finally there is the weakside linebacker. You might hear him described as the WILL linebacker. While the pass was taking up a greater share of offenses, at this stage we were still decades away from the sophisticated aerial attacks modern fans see. NFL offenses were still built more around the run. Thus defenses had to primarily focus on shutting down rushing attacks. That is done through assigning gaps to defenders. A gap is simply the space between two blockers. It can be between two offensive linemen, an offensive lineman and a blocking tight end, or a blocker and the end of the line. Defenders can be assigned either one or two gaps. Historians can’t quite agree upon whether Landry’s early 4-3 defense assigned one or two gaps to defenders. Some believe Landry’s scheme asked defensive linemen to cover two gaps. This would have the defensive tackles covering the gaps between the center and guard and the guard and tackle. Defensive ends would take the gaps between the tackle and the tight end and tight end and the end of the line (or on the weak side where the tight end would otherwise be). This gave linebackers freedom to go get the ball (even if they needed to stay disciplined and not open up cutback lanes). For a visual representation of what a two gapping 4-3 might have looked like, see the hi-tech GGN graphic below. Some historians believe the evidence points to Landry running a one gap 4-3. Defenders were responsible for a single gap. This would require the linebackers to be more limited and control specific areas of the field. The outside linebackers would need to contain and either make tackles on outside runs or at least redirect the ball carrier to the interior of the defense where there was help. Landry would have had a couple of different looks from this formation. One would require his linebacker (an all-time great named Sam Huff) to take away the run going through either gap up the middle. A visual representation can all be seen in the hi-tech GGN graphic below. In broad strokes this defense resembles some of the most common looks we see today, but the approach was different. In a league where the run was still king in offenses, defenders had to focus on first controlling and clogging their gap or gaps. Only after it was secure could they proceed to rush the quarterback. Was Landry’s originally scheme a one gapping system? Was it a two gapping system? Was it a combination of the two? Maybe one day we can try and figure it out. For now let’s move on. Of course schemes in the NFL are living, breathing organisms. Coaches are always trying to figure out news ways to exploit the weaknesses in a scheme. Landry eventually moved on to become the original head coach of the Dallas Cowboys. He adapted his 4-3, developing a version called the flex which was built to combat the Green Bay Packers’ dominant rushing attack. The 4-3 needed to adapt in other ways. In a league where offenses were still dominated by inside runs, it became too easy to have offensive guards seal off the defensive tackles and have the center shoot out to the middle linebacker at the snap. For a visual representation, see the hi-tech GGN graphic below. Soon football would see adaptations of the 4-3 to combat this. One was the Over front. The defensive line shifts to the strong side of the formation. The linemen begin the play within gaps. This makes it more difficult to wall off running lanes and puts more bodies on the side where the offense has more bodies. For a visual representation of a 4-3 Over front, you can see the hi-tech GGN graphic below. Since the linemen are beginning the play within gaps, this front makes it much more difficult to two gap. Generally speaking, linemen will play the gap in which they align. Edge contain responsibilities might fill to the defensive ends, and the linebackers might need to handle the unfilled gaps. For a visual representation of what gap assignments might look like in a 4-3 Over front, you can view the…

title: NCAA Season Preview – Quarterbacks
summary: Everyone knows that the Jets’ long term answer at quarterback likely isn’t on the roster. Even with Cade Klubnik looking okay in preseason this year, the most likely outcome is that Klubnik ends up a long-term backup. That’d be a win from a fourth-round quarterback. With that in mind, the Jets are almost certain to […]
full_text: AUSTIN, TX - APRIL 18: Quarterback Arch Manning #16 of the Texas Longhorns on the field during the Texas Longhorns Football Fan Day on April 18, 2026, at Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium in Austin, TX. (Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Everyone knows that the Jets’ long term answer at quarterback likely isn’t on the roster. Even with Cade Klubnik looking okay in preseason this year, the most likely outcome is that Klubnik ends up a long-term backup. That’d be a win from a fourth-round quarterback. With that in mind, the Jets are almost certain to take a quarterback early in the 2027 draft. In fact, with three first-round picks in their pocket, it’s very possible they trade up as high as they can to get the QB of their choice. So with college football returning this weekend, it’s time to take a quick look at the quarterbacks that Jets fans should get to know. I’ll be going over the 15 draft-eligible quarterbacks in college football that intrigue me the most. This is a comprehensive list, but does not include every draft-eligible quarterback, or even every draft prospect that other evaluators like. Simply a list of guys that I’ll have my eye on. Arch Manning, Texas Arch Manning is the top quarterback in this class until proven otherwise. Yes, he struggled at the start of last season, but he improved as the season went on. No quarterback in this class has Manning’s combination of size, athleticism, and arm strength. If a team could build a quarterback in a lab, it’d probably look like Manning. That said, he’s going to need to improve on how he played last year if he’s going to be the top pick. That’s the expectation, but not a guaranteed result. He was inaccurate compared to his peers at just a 61.4% completion. His 7.8 yards per attempt are not good enough when he’s playing with a top-3 wide receiver corps in the country. Again, he improved as the year went on, but he’s going to need to continue to improve as expected. I’ll be watching to see how quickly, if at all, Manning reaches his potential this season. Trinidad Chambliss, Ole Miss The star of the college football playoffs last season, Chambliss’ numbers say that he should be in the conversation for the top pick in this season. However, Chambliss is small at just 6 foot 1 and 205 pounds. He’s considerably older than your usual prospect at 24 years old this season, the same age as Anthony Richardson, who’s entering a contract year in the NFL. He also played in the very QB-friendly offense of Lane Kiffin. Now, Kiffin has left and Chambliss will have a chance to at least put that question to rest. But given how strong this draft class is, Chambliss is going to need a Heisman contender season to stay in consideration to be a top pick. Coming into the season, I’d probably have Chambliss going on Day 2. Dante Moore, Oregon Arch Manning may be the top pick because of his potential, but if we’re simply going off where guys are coming into the season, Moore is in the driver’s seat. Dante Moore led one of the best offenses in the country last season and would have been the #2 pick in the draft had he come out last season. However, Moore spurned the Jets and chose instead to return to college. Moore has elite accuracy, good arm strength, good athleticism, but struggles with turnovers and pressure. Not the most shocking scouting report for a top quarterback. If Moore is to be the top pick in the 2027 draft he’s going to need to cut down on his turnovers, but that’s pretty much it. Unless injuries come, expect Moore to be at the very least a top 10 pick next year. LaNorris Sellers, South Carolina Sellers came into last season as an expected top draft pick. Then he went out and massively regressed from the season before. Less accurate, fewer touchdowns, more turnovers, and significantly worse rushing ability. Still, Sellers has tools that few other quarterbacks have. He’s arguably the best athlete in this quarterback class and his arm strength can rival the best. But raw tools can only take you so far; at some point, Sellers is going to need to turn that into elite production. After his poor 2025 season, Sellers comes into this season as a likely day 3 pick. However, you simply can’t count out a guy with these kinds of tools putting together an elite season and fighting his way back into contention to be a top pick. Drew Mestemaker, Oklahoma State If you’ve never heard of Drew Mestemaker I wouldn’t blame you. The former North Texas quarterback was putting up video game numbers at a small school that nobody but college football psychos were paying attention to. However, Mestemaker made the jump to Oklahoma State in the transfer portal, and now he’s going to have a much bigger spotlight on him. Mestemaker led the NCAA in passing yards by over 500 yards last season. He led the NCAA in yards per attempt. He was second in touchdowns thrown, and he was top 10 in completion percentage. Again, all against the lesser competition that North Texas played. Be prepared to hear Josh Allen comparisons here. Mestemaker has the biggest arm in the NCAA. He’s athletic, and the same size as Allen. Mestemaker is, of course, more accurate than Allen was at this point in his career, but Allen was better out of the pocket. Mestmaker has work to do to make a name for himself as he moves into a Power-4 conference this season. That said, don’t be shocked when he comes out of nowhere to be in the conversation to be a top 5 pick this season. CJ Carr, Notre Dame NFL teams had eyes on CJ Carr all of last season. The Notre Dame quarterback was one of the breakout stars of the 2025 season as a redshirt freshman starter. His 9.4 yards per attempt were tied for fourth in the country last season with Fernando Mendoza and Diego Pavia. 24 TDs, only 6 INTs, and 66.6% completion. Carr’s best tool is his composure in the pocket and his feel for playing the position. While so many others on this list are here because of the potential to be the next unicorn star, Carr is here because his floor is exceedingly high. He simply knows how to play quarterback and showed it in a pro-style system at Notre Dame last year. If Carr is going to end up in contention to be a top-pick this season he’ll need his production to take another step up. Completion needs to jump over 70%, TDs closer to 30, and INTs to 5 or under if he can. All very possible for Carr entering his second year as a starter. Julian Sayin, Ohio State There’s no quarterback in this draft class that’s more “in the eye of the beholder” than Julian Sayin. The Ohio State quarterback was arguably the best in the country last season. He completed over 78% of his passes, threw for 31 TDs, only threw 6 interceptions, and averaged 9.3 yards per pass attempt. Those are first pick in the draft numbers. However, Sayin is small for the position at just 6 foot 1. He lacks the elite arm strength that others in this class do. He’s also not all that athletic as a pocket passer. Without those NFL tools, his production is muted in NFL Draft discussions. If Sayin comes out and wins the Heisman this year, NFL teams are going to have no choice but to recognize the talent. That said, plenty of NFL teams won’t consider a quarterback with elite technical ability but lacking in elite tools because their ceiling simply isn’t high enough for them at the top of the draft. Sam Leavitt, LSU After the 2024 season, Sam Leavitt looked like a future first-round pick, but 2025 wasn’t the season he was hoping for. He didn’t show much improvement and dealt with injuries, and as a result Leavitt wasn’t able to take advantage of the weak class in 2026. Now he comes back this season after a transfer to LSU with lower expectations than he should. Leavitt is about to be paired with elite talent on offense and a head coach in Lane Kiffin known for getting the most out of his quarterbacks. With his athleticism, Leavitt has a chance to have a special season at LSU. He has to…

title: 11 notes from today’s Eagles training camp practice
summary: Today marked the fifteenth Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. Here’s what I observed down at the Jefferson Health Training Complex! EAGLES PRACTICE NOTES ROSTER MOVES: The Eagles released veteran safety J.T. Gray (who dropped a sure interception on Saturday night) and waived/injured Ja’Quinden Jackson, who was taken off the […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JUNE 9: Elijah Moore #19 of the Philadelphia Eagles runs with the ball during mandatory minicamp at Jefferson Health Training Complex on June 9, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Today marked the fifteenth Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. Here’s what I observed down at the Jefferson Health Training Complex! EAGLES PRACTICE NOTES Relatively lighter practice today. No pads and only about 70 minutes long. EAGLES INJURY REPORT: BGN’s Alexis Chassen already wrote up the injury report but there are some developments I wanted to touch on. DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon were removed from the injury report; they were full go on Monday. The Eagles are certainly glad to have them back. Eli Stowers is now dealing with a hamstring injury. Not ideal. The rookie tight end really hasn’t had a good offseason. Without knowing the severity of his ailment, I wonder if he’ll begin the season on injured reserve/designated to return. Also not fun to see both Markel Bell (thumb/leg) and Willie Lampkin (stinger) missing practice after showing promise this summer. Hopefully nothing too serious here. Cole Wisniewski is now in the concussion protocol after missing most of the offseason due to hamstring injury issues. Tough development. Dameon Pierce (hamstring) and Byron Young (shoulder) both notably returned to practice today, albeit in a limited capacity. Early in camp, it looked like Pierce might push for RB3 … but Will Shipley has stepped up recently, as has Carson Steele. Gabe Hall got banged up late in practice. He was limping while jogging off the field to the sideline. Something to monitor. JALEN HURTS UPDATE: Hurts was up and down today. THE GOOD: QB1 found Dallas Goedert and Elijah Moore for short-to-medium gains in 7-on-7. And again in 11-on-11s. A Hurts pass over the middle to DeVonta in stride went just past the outstretched arm of a defender for first down yardage. Hurts connected with Darius Cooper over the middle. They have a nice chemistry. Good things happen when the Eagles throw the ball to DC. Hurts hit Hollywood Brown deep down the left sideline. (I should note that Jordan Davis and other defensive linemen were crashing down on the QB. Maybe he would’ve gotten the pass off in a game and taken the hit … or maybe it would’ve been a sack.) THE BAD: Hurts failed to get a throw off in 7-on-7. That used to be a more common issue for him in the past. Also rare: One of Hurts’ passes hit the fly swatter dummy, which is designed to replicate a leaping defensive lineman in 7-on-7, and went incomplete. Hurts had another throw batted down at the line of scrimmage by an actual Eagles defender in 11-on-11. Hurts overthrew Hollywood Brown deep for what should’ve been a touchdown. Brown was pretty open with Andrew Mukuba trailing. Side note: feel like this was the first practice of camp where Brown’s vertical threat ability showed up. Hurts put the ball too far out in front of DeVonta on a red zone fade throw. Cooper DeJean had tight coverage on the play. Hurts placed a pass behind Johnny Mundt on a short throw over the middle for an incompletion. It felt like Hurt’ average time to throw was longer than it’s been most of this summer. Part of that was Vic Fangio’s defense playing smothering coverage but Hurts did have his starting receivers out there today in Smith, Lemon, Dontayvion Wicks. MAKAI LEMON UPDATE: Lemon was notably working with the starting offense during his first day back. His first target resulted in an incompletion. From my angle, it looked like it may have been a drop. Others thought the throw from Hurts wasn’t on the money and/or timing may have been an issue. Later on, Lemon was utilized on a screen pass. He was also used in pre-snap motion a decent amount. I’m running out of ways to praise Jalyx Hunt. He’s had an awesome summer. It felt like he was living in the backfield today. Hunt got to Hurts for a “sack” with Dallas Goedert either blocking him one-on-one or chipping him. Hunt also beat Lane Johnson to pressure Hurts. Hunt just generally kept getting near Hurts before having to pull up. Hunt was in prime position for a TFL on Saquon Barkley. Moro Ojomo also had a nice day of disruption. He quickly beat the Eagles’ interior offensive line to likely “sack” Hurts up the middle. Dontayvion Wicks has mostly avoided drops this summer but he did have a bounce pass off his hands and well into the air before ultimately falling incomplete. Throw from Hurts may have been a tad higher than it needed to be. Elijah Moore made a number of catches today after missing the Eagles’ previous practice. He was also involved in a jet sweep that went for a chunk gain. He’s one of the the tougher players to figure out in terms of whether he’ll make the 53-man roster or not. If he does get cut, I think the Eagles would try to get him back on the practice squad and use his temporary elevations. BACKUP QUARTERBACK BATTLE UPDATE: Tanner McKee was first up as QB2 today. Nothing overly flashy but a lot of shorter completions. Felt like the ball rarely hit the ground when he was out there. Andy Dalton did have a good completion to Moore along the sideline. No major movement in this battle today. The Eagles’ defense definitely won the day. The offense stalled in the end of practice scrimmage scenario. Shout out to BGN community member MOD#92 ! I had the pleasure of meeting them at today’s practice. Our Canadian friend had a cool story about how he came to visit Philly this week. I’ll let them decide if they want to share more details or not in the comment section below. ROSTER MOVES: The Eagles released veteran safety J.T. Gray (who dropped a sure interception on Saturday night) and waived/injured Ja’Quinden Jackson, who was taken off the field in an ambulance just two days ago. UP NEXT: Here’s the upcoming schedule (all times listed Eastern): Tuesday, August 25 — Practice open to fans at Lincoln Financial Field (6:00 PM start) Wednesday, August 26 — Final training camp practice (3:00 PM start) Thursday, August 27 — Walkthrough closed to access Friday, August 28 — Eagles vs. Bengals (8:00 PM start) Saturday, August 29 — Rest day Sunday, August 30 — 53-man roster cuts deadline at 6:00 PM

title: Eagles sign two free agents
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles made four roster moves on Monday, according to the NFL’s official personnel notice. Here’s an overview: Let’s sort through this news on a player-by-player basis. JAYLEN MAHONEY The 25-year-old Mahoney played college football at Vanderbilt before signing with the San Francisco 49ers as an undrafted rookie free agent in 2024. He played […]
full_text: ORLANDO, FLORIDA - APRIL 04: Jaylen Mahoney #24 of the Orlando Storm looks on prior to a game against the Louisville Kings at Inter&Co Stadium on April 04, 2026 in Orlando, Florida. (Photo by Dustin Markland/UFL/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles made four roster moves on Monday, according to the NFL’s official personnel notice. Here’s an overview: DB Jaylen Mahoney and RB Jordan Mims were signed to the roster. S J.T. Gray was released. RB Ja’Quinden Jackson was waived/injured. Let’s sort through this news on a player-by-player basis. JAYLEN MAHONEY The 25-year-old Mahoney played college football at Vanderbilt before signing with the San Francisco 49ers as an undrafted rookie free agent in 2024. He played zero defense snaps and 30 special teams snaps as a rookie before bouncing on and off the 49ers in 2025. He also spent some time on the New York Jets’ practice squad late last season. Mahoney was selected by the Orlando Storm in the 2026 UFL Draft. He played 259 snaps for them, with most of them coming at safety. Now in Philly, Mahoney will help the Eagles fill some safety reps in practice and the preseason finale. JORDAN MIMS Mims, 23, was a 2023 undrafted rookie free agent signing by the Buffalo Bills. He’s logged 108 offensive snaps and 71 special teams snaps over three seasons in the NFL. Mims mostly recently spent time with the Minnesota Vikings, who originally signed him in late July before waiving him two weeks later. Like Mahoney, Mims is likely arriving in Philly to help fill some reps in practice and the preseason finale. J.T. GRAY The Eagles originally signed Gray, a former All-Pro special teams player, with the thought he could provide safety depth and help out on Michael Clay’s unit. But he didn’t do much to stand out this offseason and now he’s gone. JA’QUINDEN JACKSON The Eagles originally signed Jackson when they were dealing with some running back injuries in training camp. Jackson got hurt on the opening kickoff of Saturday’s Eagles preseason game against the New England Patriots and was taken off the field in an ambulance. After a visit to the hospital, Jackson was able to travel back to Philly with the team.

title: Eagles-Patriots Film Review: Encouraging signs from the backup offensive line
summary: Reminder: it’s preseason! However, the film still provided useful information about the Eagles’ offensive line depth. The second-string line bullied the Patriots’ backup defensive front throughout the opening drives, both individually and collectively. Drew Kendall, Willie Lampkin and Markel Bell all produced impressive moments, so I quite enjoyed this one because of this. The Eagles […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 22: Willie Lampkin #61 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on during the national anthem prior to an NFL preseason football game against the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Reminder: it’s preseason! However, the film still provided useful information about the Eagles’ offensive line depth. The second-string line bullied the Patriots’ backup defensive front throughout the opening drives, both individually and collectively. Drew Kendall, Willie Lampkin and Markel Bell all produced impressive moments, so I quite enjoyed this one because of this. The Eagles appear to have an absurd amount of young talent along the interior. A few schematic details were also worth monitoring. The Eagles used several C-gap insert concepts, with a receiver coming inside to block through the C-gap (the gap to the outside shoulder of the tackle). The Rams have used this frequently in recent seasons, and Mannion appears interested in incorporating it here. Even on the first offensive snap, Darius Cooper ran a deep route through the C-gap. It is only preseason, but this feels like a feature of the new offense. I forgot to clip up the Cooper route, so shoutout to Devin Jackson for supplying the goods… They showed a look off of it! First offensive play of the game, the #Eagles sent Darius Cooper through the C-gap and looks like he ran a corner route. Was just covered well by the Patriots. https://t.co/wg3y3MoJob pic.twitter.com/3ljXhTVEiW — Devin Jackson (@RealD_Jackson) August 23, 2026 The opening clip summarizes the positive side of the game perfectly. Outside zone requires the entire offensive line to work together, and the Eagles’ backup unit was excellent here. The initial movement created horizontal displacement across the front, while the individual blocks remained connected long enough for Will Shipley to press the run through the B-gap for a nice gain. Markel Bell looks so strong in his upper body, and he tosses the edge out of the club to create a huge hole. Shipley deserves credit, too. He carried 11 times for 56 yards and a touchdown, running with good vision and decisiveness behind the backup line. The blocking made his job easier, but he consistently identified the available lane and ran hard through contact. He looks a decent fit for this new outside zone world that we are living in. The bigger takeaway is the work of offensive line coach Chris Kuper. A lot of these outside-zone principles are relatively new to this group, yet the line already looks comfortable working in unison. When outside zone is executed this cleanly, it remains one of the most satisfying concepts to watch. It doesn’t get much better than this. Eagles' Offense All22 vs Patriots (Preseason Week 2). 1) Shoutout OL coach Chris Kuper, because this is outstanding. So many great individual blocks, but as a collective, it doesn't get much better. Outside zone, when run this well, is a beautiful thing. Will Shipley played well… pic.twitter.com/UTpKF8Q5GT — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) August 23, 2026 The success of the running game created opportunities for Mannion to build easy answers off the same presentation. This is a straightforward under-center play-action concept, with the action flowing away from outside zone before Andy Dalton finds Darius Cooper in space. Football does not always need to be complicated. If the defense respects the run action, the offense should be willing to take the simple completion. Cooper’s athleticism does the rest. He makes the linebacker miss immediately and turns an easy throw into a much larger gain. Cooper finished with three receptions for 44 yards on four targets, and his movement skills stood out whenever the ball reached him in space. He looks very fluid and powerful as a route runner and with the ball in his hands. This is the type of sequencing I want to see from the Eagles. Establish the outside-zone action, force the linebackers to react, and then attack the space created by their movement. The regular-season defense will not always make it this easy, but the relationship between the run and pass concepts is encouraging. It’s something we just haven’t seen enough of (or at times, at all) in recent years. 2) Darius Cooper looked good, and his athleticism on this play stands out. He does a great job making the LB miss and creating extra yards after the catch. Also, how nice is it to see under center PA away from outside zone? Football doesn't always have to be complicated when… pic.twitter.com/6xqdwGCZDN — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) August 23, 2026 Markel Bell’s best snaps are incredibly physical, but there are still moments where the rawness of his game becomes evident. He loses this rep and allows penetration, contributing to a two-yard loss. I did like Eli Stowers’ willingness to block the cornerback on the perimeter. It is not a dominant rep, but he competes and gives the runner an opportunity. He still didn’t block well in this one, but the effort was there. The real reason to highlight the play, though, is Willie Lampkin. His finish is outstanding. Lampkin’s size will always lead to questions about how he will look against starting defensive linemen, but his competitiveness is impossible to miss. He was one of the most impressive Eagles in the first preseason game and continued to make his presence felt against the Patriots. The Eagles’ starting offensive line better play well early, because if Cam Jurgens or Landon Dickerson play like they did last year, these backups will be ready to take away their jobs. 3) You can still see some of the raw elements of Markel Bell's game at times (not surprising for a rookie) as he loses here. Although it's against a CB, it is still good to see Stowers willingness to block here, too. However, the only real reason I'm posting this one, is to… pic.twitter.com/BZkPWWvnyv — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) August 23, 2026 Cooper’s second reception is even more encouraging because it demonstrates traits that can translate against better competition and fit this scheme well. Mannion has shown an interest in attacking the middle of the field, which emphasizes receivers who can separate and finish catches without allowing the ball into their frame as you may take a hit. Cooper runs a sharp route and plucks the ball cleanly away from his frame before protecting himself from the arriving defender. He has the awareness and athleticism to avoid the bigger hit. There was not a huge amount to learn about the Eagles’ receivers in this game, but Cooper helped himself. He was one of the few pass-catchers who consistently created something when given an opportunity. 4) This is exactly what you want to see out of Darius Cooper. We know that Mannion is going to call more middle of the field stuff, so this is a really nice rep. Cooper runs a good route and plucks the ball away from his frame before avoiding a big hit. A lot to like here. pic.twitter.com/3MtH0bawtK — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) August 23, 2026 Drew Kendall was the standout of the offensive line for me this week. Bell and Lampkin were the most obvious performers in the opening preseason game, but Kendall produced several outstanding blocks against the Patriots. He looked awesome at times. This combination block with Lampkin is close to perfect. They secure the defensive lineman together before Kendall works to the second level without sacrificing the initial block. These details make the Eagles’ interior depth so exciting. Kendall and Lampkin play with excellent awareness of leverage and timing, and they already look comfortable passing defenders between them. Even Jake Majors made several encouraging plays. Stowers also deserves another mention here. His block isn’t especially pretty, but his willingness is evident again. The battle for the fourth tight end spot remains up for grabs. I have liked what both EJ Jenkins and Cameron Latu have shown…

summary: Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Eagles 53-man roster 2.0: Where things stand for Willie Lampkin, Joshua Weru a week ahead of cut-down day – PHLYRunning back (3): Saquon Barkley, Tank Bigsby, Will Shipley. full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 22: Carson Steele #34 of the Philadelphia Eagles jumps over Eric Butler #30 of the New England Patriots to score a touchdown during the second half of the preseason game between the Philadelphia Eagles and the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Maddie Meyer/Getty Images) | Getty Images Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Eagles 53-man roster 2.0: Where things stand for Willie Lampkin, Joshua Weru a week ahead of cut-down day – PHLY Running back (3): Saquon Barkley, Tank Bigsby, Will Shipley. Carson Steele’s impressive showing against the New England Patriots opens up the possibility that he could be a surprise inclusion on the 53-man roster, especially if Sean Mannion does have plans to eventually implement a fullback into his newly installed scheme. (It’s not something we’ve seen yet, but that doesn’t mean it won’t eventually become part of the plan.) My thinking with Steele is there’s probably not room on the roster for both him and a fourth tight end. More on that in a moment … In Roob’s Observations: Mike Vrabel’s insight on what makes the Eagles elite – NBCSP THE CRAZY HURDLING MADMAN CARSON STEELE: How do you not love this kid? To put Carson Steele’s 6-catch, 88-yard receiving performance Saturday night into some perspective, the most yards he ever had in a college game was 57 in Ball State’s 20-16 loss to Eastern Michigan in Muncie, Ind., in 2022. The most he’s had in an NFL regular-season game is nine, in the Chiefs’ 2024 win over the Panthers in Charlotte, N.C. Steele’s 88 yards were the most by an Eagles running back in a preseason game since Raheem Mostert had 93 against the Jets (along with 69 rushing yards) in a loss to the Jets in East Rutherford in 2015. Steele, who finished at UCLA after two years at Ball State, really shined Saturday night. He showed soft hands, a great feel for running in space and tremendous toughness in traffic as well as plus athleticism hurdling defenders twice, including on his touchdown. You never want to get carried away with strong preseason perrformances against backups, but there’s a lot to like about Steele’s game. Steele spent his first couple years with the Chiefs and played in all 17 games in 2024, rushing 56 times for 183 yards with seven catches for 26 yards. There isn’t a roster spot for him here, but assuming the Eagles can get him through waivers he’s precisely the kind of player you want on the practice squad. Smart, tough and productive. Eagles 53-man roster projection 3.0: What will Howie Roseman do with Andy Dalton? – The Athletic Kubena (3): Saquon Barkley, Tank Bigsby, Will Shipley. Carson Steele just made it very hard for the Eagles to stash him on their practice squad. The hurdling Steele played like all the other 31 teams were watching — and, indeed, their pro scouting departments were. Steele, an undrafted rookie in 2024, will be subject to waivers if the Eagles cut him. I can’t see him making the roster in this crowded position group, and he has not been practicing as an H-back in training camp, suggesting the Eagles wouldn’t file him under the “tight end/fullback” category. This happens in training camp. Steele’s preseason appearances are essentially job interviews with other teams. He’ll have another one in the preseason finale on Friday against the Cincinnati Bengals. Berman (3): Saquon Barkley, Tank Bigsby, Will Shipley. This is a quality trio. Barkley is one of the best running backs in the NFL; Bigsby is one of the better No. 2 running backs. If Shipley is third on the depth chart, that’s a good depth chart. The Eagles could stash a veteran such as Dameon Pierce on the practice squad for injury insurance. Eagles-Patriots snap counts: Joshua Weru records first NFL sack in second-ever football game of his life – BGN Seeing Joshua Weru log an NFL sack in the second-ever football game of his entire life was really, really cool. Also heartwarming to see how his teammates were so happy for him. Weru has probably shown too much potential for the Eagles to expose him to waivers, which is crazy to think about. Disney announces NFL crossover with iconic characters for all 32 teams – SB Nation Philadelphia Eagles: Doctor Doom (MCU). NFL Preseason Week 2 Recap: Immediate fantasy football takeaways from Saturday’s games – PFF More concerns for Eli Stowers: Stowers played only a part-time role for the Eagles in this game. Philadelphia selected Stowers in the second round with the expectation that he could become the team’s lead tight end in 2027, with Dallas Goedert entering the final season of his contract. There was at least some hope that Stowers could contribute as a rookie. He is primarily a receiving tight end, and it has become clear that Johnny Mundt will likely serve as the second tight end in 12 personnel this season. Last week, Stowers was the second tight end in 12 personnel behind Grant Calcaterra, suggesting Stowers was fourth on the depth chart. This week, Philadelphia rested its top two tight ends, while Calcaterra was sidelined by an injury. Rather than giving Stowers an every-down role, the Eagles used him exclusively in 11 personnel during the first quarter. Philadelphia used 12 personnel on half of its plays during that stretch, with E.J. Jenkins and Cameron Latu handling the tight end snaps in those formations. Stowers should still make the roster given his draft capital, but his preseason usage has been discouraging, and his dynasty value should continue to fall. Getting Some Answers – Iggles Blitz There is still a lot of work to be done, but so far Bell looks like he’s worthy of getting a chance at RT next year. The pro game doesn’t look too fast for him. And we know he’s got the size/strength to handle defenders at any level. Bell is a beast. Tyler Steen is having the best camp of his career. He was a bit of an unknown last season. He’s playing well right now and could turn into an above average starter. This is a contract year for him so the timing is ideal from his perspective. The final OL note is that new coach Chris Kuper seems to be doing a good job. We’ve seen progress from fringe guys, rookies, young players and veterans. Everyone seems to be buying into the new system. Following in the footsteps of Jeff Stoutland isn’t easy. Kuper is off to a good start. Willie Lampkin made his name as a wrestling champion. For his next act, he’s become one of the Eagles’ best camp stories. – Inquirer “I call him a bowling ball of knives, ’cause he’s so short, he’s so small, he’s so stubby, but he is so quick and powerful and precise with his hands that for a taller guy like me, it gives me a lot of trouble,” Jordan Davis said. “It gives me a lot of fits. That’s one of the things that keeps me up at night with Willie. “He has a certain tenacity about him when he goes and plays a game.” That tenacity, according to Lampkin, is rooted in his wrestling background. Lampkin began wrestling as a freshman at Mulberry High School in Mulberry, Fla., a city in central Florida with a population of roughly 4,000. Within three years, he finished as the heavyweight runner-up in the state tournament, and within four, he won the title. He ultimately chose to pursue football over wrestling in college, playing three seasons at Coastal Carolina and two at UNC before moving on to the NFL as an undrafted free agent. But as he vies for a depth spot on the Eagles’ initial 53-man roster as an undersized, undrafted interior offensive lineman, Lampkin continues to channel the mentality and the skill set he cultivated through wrestling. “I feel like wrestling just helped me to be more gritty and just try to get after everybody,” Lampkin said. 2026 Philadelphia Eagles: Projecting final 53-man roster – ESPN Tight ends (4) — Dallas Goedert, Eli Stowers, Johnny Mundt, Grant Calcaterra. Stowers, the team’s 2026 second-round pick, still needs some seasoning — particularly as a blocker. With…

title: Eagles-Patriots snap counts: Joshua Weru records first NFL sack in second-ever football game of his life
summary: The official snap counts from the Philadelphia Eagles’ preseason loss to the New England Patriots are in. Let’s take a look. OFFENSE DEFENSE SPECIAL TEAMS DID NOT PLAY
full_text: Aug 22, 2026; Foxborough, Massachusetts, USA; Philadelphia Eagles linebacker Jose Ramirez (43) and linebacker Joshua Weru (46) sack New England Patriots quarterback Behren Morton (15) during the second half at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Gregory Fisher-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The official snap counts from the Philadelphia Eagles’ preseason loss to the New England Patriots are in. Let’s take a look. OFFENSE The Eagles took a long look at Jake Majors, who has seen a good amount of second-team reps in camp. He started at right guard and played 18 snaps there before shifting over to center for the rest of the game. Majors seems to be on the roster bubble. I’d lean towards him being off the team since he played so much on Saturday night. Majors has looked better in the games than he has in training camp practices. Quez Watkins played the most of any skill player and saw three targets that resulted in zero catches. Micah Morris is showing enough to where the Eagles shouldn’t want to expose him to waivers. Carson Steele saw a sizeable workload in part because the Eagles only dressed three running backs for this game: him, Will Shipley, and Ja’Quinden Jackson (who got hurt on the first play of the game). Steele ran hard but finished with just 33 yards on 11 carries (2.8 average). He did most of his damage as a pass-catcher to lead the Eagles in receiving with seven targets that resulted in six catches, 84 yards, and one touchdown. Steele looked awesome hurdling not one but two different defenders. Maybe the Eagles keep four ball carriers, especially if Steele can contribute in a fullback role? Steele played less on special teams in this game than he did in the first one but I wonder if that was related to the Eagles being so thin at running back. Myles Hinton has exclusively played left tackle through two preseason games despite previously getting reps at both guard spots in practice. It’s really hard to get a read on the Eagles’ QB2 situation. Andy Dalton getting two straight preseason starts seems like a good sign for his stock … but he just hasn’t played well. Tanner McKee has hardly been lights out but he’s at least been better than Dalton. There’s been speculation that the Eagles are showcasing Dalton and/or McKee for trade purposes but prioritizing a meager return over actually getting the top backup quarterback option prepared for the season seems very silly at this point. To me, McKee should be the choice of the two. While McKee hasn’t inspired a ton of confidence this summer, his previous peaks are just better than whatever the best of Dalton (who turns 38 in October) can muster at this point in time. Stone Smartt did not play on offense in the Eagles’ first preseason game. He was their second-most targeted player in their second preseason game. He also still played a lot on special teams. Seems like a practice squad candidate. Eli Stowers’ two targets resulted in zero catches. He was open for first down yardage early in the game but Dalton simply overtherw him. The rookie tight end has been targeted five times in the preseason for three catches and 12 yards. Will Shipley had a nice night, aided by the Eagles’ backup offensive line mauling the Patriots’ defense. Even so, Shipley ran hard to finish with 11 carries for 56 yards (5.1 average) and one touchdown. Shipley also looked good working with the Eagles’ starting offense against the Pats in joint practices last week. He’s earned his RB3 role. Britain Covey’s sole catch went for a 14-yard touchdown. He muffed a punt return but was ultimately able to get back on the ball. In the first preseason game, Willie Lampkin played four snaps at center and 19 at right guard. On Saturday night, Lampkin took all of his 18 snaps at center. And he looked pretty great while doing it. He’s clearly making the roster. Last week, Drew Kendall saw four snaps at right guard and six at center. This week, Kendall logged all 18 of his snaps at left guard. Guessing he’ll be the top interior backup option, even ahead of Lampkin. Darius Cooper, who is awesome, was the Eagles’ top graded offensive player by Pro Football Focus standards. He caught three of his four targets (the only missed connection was a Dalton overthrow) for 44 yards. It was good to see the Eagles only used him for 18 snaps before then resting him. Cooper previously played 29 snaps (66%) in the first preseason game. There’s really no need to further expose him to injury in the preseason at this point. We can see that he’s good and deserves a role in the offense. Zeke Correll logged 16 snaps despite only signing with the Eagles on Friday. Must be tough to play without even practicing with the team at all. Cole Payton was limited to just three snaps, all of which came with less than a minute remaining in the game. We should see plenty of him in the preseason finale. DEFENSE Not sure there’s room for Gabe Hall on the roster but he deserves to make the team based on merit. He looked pretty good against the Pats as both a run defender and pass rusher. Speaking of defensive tackles who look good, man, how about Ty Robinson? He had a terrible start to camp before really turning it around recently. Through two preseason games, he’s produced three sacks, four TFLs, and four quarterback hits (he also had another QB hit wiped out by a Kelee Ringo penalty). Kudos to Robinson for responding in a big way after likely feeling the pressure to perform. The 2025 fourth-round pick will begin the season as the fifth defensive tackle behind Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, Moro Ojomo, and Byron Young. Maybe he eventually pushes for the DT4 role but Vic Fangio seems to like “BY” much more than Robinson. Jose Ramirez has popped a bit on both defense and special teams in the preseason. Could be a practice squad guy. Shaun Wade has had some struggles in coverage but two forced fumbles through two preseason games is impressive. You have to appreciate his hustle. Kapena Gushiken did not see any playing time at safety in this game after taking 10 snaps there last week. His action against the Pats was limited to being a slot corner/box defender. The Gush is making a push for a roster spot as a development version of Michael Carter II, a hybrid nickel/safety. Zion Wilson has exceeded low expectations this summer. Seems like a good developmental guy to keep around on the practice squad. Seeing Joshua Weru log an NFL sack in the second-ever football game of his entire life was really, really cool. Also heartwarming to see how his teammates were so happy for him. Weru has probably shown too much potential for the Eagles to expose him to waivers, which is crazy to think about. Seems like Smael Mondon Jr. has been used as a blitzer a lot through these two preseason games. Is that because the Eagles think he’s good in that role and/or is it about wanting to test out his skills in that capacity? Chance Campbell only played 32 snaps but finished second on the Eagles in total tackles with seven. The Eagles are truly deep at off-ball linebacker. Good to see Cole Wisniewski make his Eagles preseason debut. He’s missed most of the offseason due to injury but maybe he can make a strong final push to be the fourth safety. Mac McWilliams didn’t look great and then got banged up. Not good. Uar Bernard logged two assisted tackles, the first game-action football tackles of his entire life. Slowly but surely making progress in his development. Don’t think we’ll be seeing Arnold Ebiketie or A.J. Epenesa in the Eagles’ third preseason game. They clearly look overqualified to be playing against backups, as they should. The Eagles have strong depth at edge rusher. Vic Fangio has said there’s still an ongoing competition between Marcus Epps and Michael Carter II at safety … but Epps not even playing in the preseason games while MC2 does play really tells you the former is going to be the starter. title: Former Steelers WR announces retirement from NFL

Robinson was drafted in the second round of the 2014 NFL Draft by the Jacksonville Jaguars. In just his second season, he proved to be one of the […]
full_text: Former Pittsburgh Steelers wide receiver Allen Robinson has announced his retirement from the NFL. The Penn State product finishes his career with 564 catches and 43 touchdowns. Robinson was drafted in the second round of the 2014 NFL Draft by the Jacksonville Jaguars. In just his second season, he proved to be one of the game’s top receivers, catching 80 passes for 1,400 yards and a league-leading 14 touchdowns. He then caught 73 passes in 2016, as Jacksonville went on a Cinderella run to the AFC Championship Game. After suffering a season-ending injury in the first game of the 2017 season, Robinson signed with the Chicago Bears, where he would spend the next four years of his career, putting up a pair of 1,000-yard seasons. He had a one-year stint with the Los Angeles Rams in 2022 before signing with the Steelers in 2023, catching 34 passes for 280 yards. He last played in a regular season game in 2024 with the Detroit Lions. Let us know what you think in the comments . full_text: The Pittsburgh Steelers are getting closer to seeing their first-round pick on the field in game action for the first time. Right tackle Max Iheanachor told the media on Monday that the team is planning for him to play against the Buffalo Bills on Thursday. Iheanachor hasn’t appeared in either of the Steelers’ first two preseason games. He suffered an injury at training camp on August 6 and is believed to have affected his upper body. Today was the first day Iheanachor practiced since sustaining the injury. Iheanachor said he wanted to come back earlier, but wants to suit up before the exhibitions end. “I wanted to play since the first preseason [game], but obviously missing practices and stuff,” Iheanachor said, per ESPN reporter Brooke Pryor . “Couldn’t get out there with the guys. So I mean, that’s the plan to play this last one.” The Steelers selected Iheanachor, feet away from Acrisure Stadium, with the 21st pick out of Arizona State to bolster their offensive line. Pittsburgh’s offensive line has struggled to find cohesiveness throughout the preseason. Dylan Cook and Broderick Jones have split time at right tackle with Cook primarily playing with the first-team. Two Steelers rookie OL, Max Iheanachor and Gennings Dunker, are back at practice pic.twitter.com/oSZto7NYHU — Nick Farabaugh (@FarabaughFB) August 24, 2026 Iheanachor is listed as the backup right tackle behind Cook. The Steelers are only planning on developing Iheanachor on the right side after flipping Troy Fautanu to the left. The Steelers play their final preseason game and only road contest against the Buffalo Bills in the new Highmark Stadium on Thursday, August 27. Let us know what you think in the comments . summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers got a double shot of good injury news on Monday. Additionally, Jalen Ramsey was activated off the PUP list after not practicing at all in Latrobe. Speaking […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PA - NOVEMBER 02: Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Jalen Ramsey (5) talks to Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. (24) during the NFL football game between the Indianapolis Colts and Pittsburgh Steelers on November 02, 2025 at Acrisure Stadium in Pittsburgh, PA. (Photo by Mark Alberti/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers got a double shot of good injury news on Monday. Rookie offensive tackle Max Iheanachor returned to practice after missing north of two weeks with an injury sustained earlier in the month during training camp. Additionally, Jalen Ramsey was activated off the PUP list after not practicing at all in Latrobe. Speaking to the media for the first time since returning, Ramsey went to bat for his teammate, Joey Porter Jr, who is currently seeking a contract extension ahead of the final year on his rookie contract. “We need the whole secondary,” Ramsey said via Nick Farabaugh of PennLive . “They need to pay Joey Porter Jr.” Ramsey added that he is completely behind Porter and in his corner through the process. “I’m overly in Joey’s corner,” Ramsey added via Jack Hillgrove . “Joey needs to get compensated for being a valuable part of this secondary and a valuable part of this defense and team.” Earlier on Monday, head coach Mike McCarthy said that the team and Porter were at “an impasse” when it comes to contract talks. ”I learned this in my early years as a head coach, you have to separate the business and football. Sometimes it’s easier in others,” McCarthy said Monday. “ This is a challenge for both Joey and us because we’re first-year staff. We’ve seen them play, compete against Joey. I would love the opportunity to coach Joey Porter. I know our defensive guys would love the opportunity. So we’re at an impasse right here, and you got to respect that. Every one of us has a contract. The organization, they have beliefs and so forth. But yeah, that’s just kind of where we are.” The Steelers traditionally do not negotiate contracts once the regular season begins. They could use the franchise tag on Porter ahead of free agency in March, which would give them another offseason to work out a long-term deal. Let us know what you think in the comments . title: Mike McCarthy: Steelers at an ‘impasse’ with Joey Porter Jr.
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers got some good news Monday morning as head coach Mike McCarthy announced that both rookie tackle Max Iheanachor and defensive back Jalen Ramsey will return to practice this week ahead of their final preseason game against the Buffalo Bills. This will be the first time Ramsey has been cleared to practice since […]
full_text: The Pittsburgh Steelers got some good news Monday morning as head coach Mike McCarthy announced that both rookie tackle Max Iheanachor and defensive back Jalen Ramsey will return to practice this week ahead of their final preseason game against the Buffalo Bills. This will be the first time Ramsey has been cleared to practice since the start of training camp after landing on the PUP list. But this good news was also undercut with a more troubling update. Joey Porter Jr., lir Ramsey, spent the entirety of training camp in the PUP List, reportedly dealing with a back issue. He’s still also seeking a contract extension from the Steelers. On Monday, the Steelers head coach admitted that the Porter Jr. contract talks have reached an impasse. “I learned this in my early years as a head coach, you have to separate the business and football. Sometimes it’s easier in others. This is a challenge for both Joey and us because we’re first-year staff,” McCarthy said Monday. “We’ve seen them play, compete against Joey. I would love the opportunity to coach Joey Porter. I know our defensive guys would love the opportunity. So we’re at an impasse right here, and you got to respect that. Every one of us has a contract. The organization, they have beliefs and so forth. But yeah, that’s just kind of where we are.” ESPN’s Brooke Pryor reported over the weekend that there hasn’t been any meaningful progress in contract negotiations between Porter Jr. and the Steelers. With the start of the regular season now under three weeks away, questions about whether or not the star defensive back will be willing to play without a new deal from the Steelers will continue to come up. The Steelers typically don’t negotiate contracts with players in the middle of the season, so it’s reasonable to expect September 13, the date of the Steelers’ Week 1 matchup with the Falcons to serve as a hard deadline. Time is running out, but Steelers fans should remember that negotiations with T.J. Watt in 2021 also went right up until the 11th hour. That year, Watt signed his extension just three days before the Week 1 kickoff. Whether a similar deal can be struck with Porter Jr. remains to be seen. Let us know what you think in the comments . title: A Seahawks 53-man roster projection entering preseason finale
summary: We’ve reached the final week of the 2026 NFL preseason. The Seattle Seahawks have some interesting decisions to make come Aug. 30, and the injuries to Jake Bobo, Bud Clark, and Mason Richman will surely change the equation a bit as far as who makes the team and which bubble players now have a better […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - AUGUST 15: Montorie Foster Jr. #87 of the Seattle Seahawks reacts during the first quarter during the NFL preseason game against the Dallas Cowboys at Lumen Field on August 15, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Jack Compton/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’ve reached the final week of the 2026 NFL preseason. The Seattle Seahawks have some interesting decisions to make come Aug. 30, and the injuries to Jake Bobo, Bud Clark, and Mason Richman will surely change the equation a bit as far as who makes the team and which bubble players now have a better chance to survive final cuts. Before we look ahead to the Kansas City Chiefs finale, let’s get to another Seahawks 53-man roster projection! As always, this is purely an initial 53 and not a season-long projection. Offense (25) Quarterback (3): Sam Darnold, Drew Lock, Jalen Milroe Cut: N/A Notes : Yes, I’m keeping Milroe for now. It’s a little more tenuous than the previous week and I’m questioning whether or not he’s a roster certainty. However, he’s still in year two of a third-round rookie contract, which means his cap charge is all of $1.4 million this season. Basically, if Milroe is let go it has a lot more to do with needing his spot for a position of greater need, because there is no real cap relief that comes with giving up now. Running Back (3): Jadarian Price (R), Emanuel Wilson, George Holani Cut: Jacardia Wright, Velus Jones Jr PUP: Zach Charbonnet Notes : I thought about keeping Jacardia Wright on the 53-man roster, but one huge touchdown run shouldn’t be enough to put him over the top after missing much of camp due to injury. The one hedge I have is the health of Emanuel Wilson, who didn’t play in the Titans game and has been out of practice with his own injury. Wilson should be comfortably on the roster, but if his availability in the coming weeks is in doubt, Wright could be added to the fold. Fullback (1): Brady Russell Cut: Brock Lampe Already on IR: Robbie Ouzts Notes : I have no doubt that Russell will be on the roster, but he’s also not a traditional fullback. Seattle may scour the market for fullbacks and/or keep Lampe on the practice squad. I’m admittedly unsure whether or not Seattle rosters two fullbacks. Wide Receiver (5): Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Cooper Kupp, Rashid Shaheed, Tory Horton, Montorie Foster Cut: Emmanuel Henderson Jr (R), Cody White, Ricky White III, Irv Charles, Rashad Rochelle Notes : The Jake Bobo injury has changed the equation. I think Foster, even with the pre-snap penalty issues, has done enough to make his way into the roster. Cody White clears waivers all the time so I’m not worried if he’s waived. Emmanuel Henderson Jr could be a surprise sixth wide receiver over everyone else for his value as a special teams gunner. Maybe he’s the real Dareke Young replacement, which Ricky White may not seem to be. Tight End (4): A.J. Barner, Elijah Arroyo, Eric Saubert , Nick Kallerup Cut: Nick Vannett Notes : If the Seahawks keep five at wide receiver then they might as well keep four at tight end. This would be the same quartet as last season. Offensive Line (9) : Charles Cross, Abe Lucas, Josh Jones, Anthony Bradford, Olu Oluwatimi, Jalen Sundell, Grey Zabel, Christian Haynes , Beau Stephens (R) Cut: Federico Maranges, Bobby Hart , Amari Kight, Logan Brown, Bryce Cabeldue IR: Mason Richman Notes : I don’t think anyone needs to replace Richman now that he’s surely done for the season . I’m banking on Haynes being the primary backup guard, with Beau Stephens as the third-string guard. Any thought of Olu Oluwatimi possibly getting dealt so that Richman could be the new backup center was thrown out the window on Sunday. Hart likely is a veteran option on the practice squad. Defense (25) Defensive Line (6): Byron Murphy II, Leonard Williams, Jarran Reed, Rylie Mills, Mike Morris , Brandon Pili Cut: J.R. Singleton, Bubba Thomas , Uso Seumalo (R) , Deven Eastern (R) Notes : Unless there’s some sort of trade value to be had with Morris on an expiring deal, I think they have their core three of Murphy, Leo, and Reed, with Mills as the situational pass rusher and Morris as the jack-of-all-trades guy who can play in sub-packages and garbage time. Pili is the nose tackle who takes up 5-10 snaps a game when he’s active. I wouldn’t be surprised, however, if Pili is a practice squad stash again. Outside Linebacker (4): Derick Hall, Uchenna Nwosu , Dante Fowler Jr, DeMarcus Lawrence Cut: Jared Ivey, Connor O’Toole , Marvin Jones Jr (R), Jamie Sheriff, Jalan Gaines , Aidan Hubbard (R) Notes : If a fifth true edge makes it, I think O’Toole is that fifth guy. Ivey has shown almost nothing between camp in preseason for me to think he gets a roster spot this year. Sheriff played well on Sunday but I don’t think he’s in an advantageous position having missed so much camp time. Inside Linebacker (5): Ernest Jones IV, Drake Thomas, Tyrice Knight, Patrick O’Connell , Chazz Surratt Cut: Chris Paul Jr, Aaron Smith , Power Echols Notes : I think the top four are locks and it’s just a matter of whether or not Surratt is so valuable on special teams that they want to keep him on the 53 versus calling him up from the practice squad. Seattle values ST players enough to maybe roster a guy or two whom otherwise wouldn’t touch regular season snaps on offense or defense. Cornerback (5): Devon Witherspoon, Josh Jobe, Nehemiah Pritchett , Julian Neal (R), Noah Igbinoghene Cut: Jordan Washington (R), Michael Dansby (R), Andre Fuller (R) , Trevon Diggs Notes : We are TBD on Terrion Arnold so I’ll leave him off until he’s signed and placed on the exempt list. I think Igbinoghene has looked really good throughout preseason and in the training camp practices I attended. Trevon Diggs is battling for a roster spot and I think Seattle could end up giving him the practice squad treatment after this last week of preseason. He shouldn’t be subject to waivers and could just sign to the PS after the deadline. If a rookie is to make the team outside of Julian Neal, it might be Fuller for what he can provide in the slot. Safety (5): Julian Love, Ty Okada, Nick Emmanwori, A.J. Finley , D’Anthony Bell Cut: Maxen Hook, Rodney Thomas II IR: Bud Clark Notes : Well, Bud Clark is not back any time soon . Emmanwori is off PUP and unless he’s had a setback I don’t see why he’d go on IR if he has to miss the start of the regular season. Finley and Bell have been the predominant safeties through the early portions of both preseason games. Bell may be the backup for Emmanwori as that box safety, whereas Finley would be the deep safety filling in as Okada’s backup/Clark’s replacement. Special Teams (3) Kicker (1) : Jason Myers Punter (1) : Michael Dickson Long Snapper (1) : Chris Stoll Cut: No one Notes : Nothing to debate here. We’ll have another roster projection later in the week from Bryce Coutts, and maybe we’ll sneak in a final one after the Chiefs game on Friday. You can do your own 53-man roster projection in The Feed , much like the one done by HamsterG!

summary: The Seattle Seahawks brought on former All-Pro Trevon Diggs to compete in their cornerback room. While Diggs did not play against the Tennessee Titans, we may see him in Friday’s preseason finale against the Kansas City Chiefs. Once upon a time, Diggs was good enough to warrant a five-year, $97 million contract extension from the […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - DECEMBER 25: Trevon Diggs #7 of the Dallas Cowboys signs autographs after the game against the Washington Commanders at Northwest Stadium on December 25, 2025 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by G Fiume/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks brought on former All-Pro Trevon Diggs to compete in their cornerback room. While Diggs did not play against the Tennessee Titans, we may see him in Friday’s preseason finale against the Kansas City Chiefs. Once upon a time, Diggs was good enough to warrant a five-year, $97 million contract extension from the Dallas Cowboys. At this stage of Diggs’ career, he’s looking to make a 53-man roster again. As such, his Seahawks contract is as straightforward and cheap as you could possibly get for someone of his caliber and experience. OverTheCap.com has the Diggs contract details. This is the veteran’s minimum salary for someone who has as many credited seasons as Diggs. While he has seven accrued seasons, he has six credited seasons due to playing just two regular season games in 2023 before his season-ending ACL tear. That’s a difference of $85,000 in minimum salary. There is no signing bonus for Diggs and it sounds like no game-based incentives based on prior reporting. The Seahawks could cut or trade Diggs by the end of this week and assume zero dead money. This is as low-risk a signing as you can get, and it also means Diggs is not remotely guaranteed a roster spot. If/when Terrion Arnold signs with the Seahawks, that might be a more interesting contract to look at.

title: 5 key observations from Seahawks vs. Titans snap counts
summary: The Seattle Seahawks are two-thirds of the way through what has probably been the most lackluster preseason under Mike Macdonald. I think we can deal with an underwhelming August when it’s coming off the back of a little achievement called winning the Super Bowl. Anyway, the snap counts have come out for Seattle’s 19-16 loss […]
full_text: Aug 23, 2026; Nashville, Tennessee, USA; Tennessee Titans wide receiver Xavier Restrepo (87) makes a catch in front of Seattle Seahawks cornerback Andre Fuller (35) during the first half at Nissan Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Steve Roberts-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Seattle Seahawks are two-thirds of the way through what has probably been the most lackluster preseason under Mike Macdonald. I think we can deal with an underwhelming August when it’s coming off the back of a little achievement called winning the Super Bowl . Anyway, the snap counts have come out for Seattle’s 19-16 loss to the Tennessee Titans. Playing more isn’t necessarily a good thing in terms of making the roster, but the context of those snap counts can be crucial clues in identifying who’s got the onside track to make the 53. Seattle Seahawks offensive snap counts Bobby Hart pretty much goes the distance It’s notable that Amari Kight (for whatever reason, probably injury related) did not play any snaps. Hart is a veteran swing tackle whose track record as a starter is… well it’s not good, but he’s here to be depth and maybe even chill on the practice squad after cuts are made. In the first half, Hart was right tackle and Josh Jones was left tackle, then he flipped to left tackle with Jalen Milroe in the second half. By the way, the Mason Richman injury likely extended Christian Haynes’ night (hence the 37 snaps) and moved up Bryce Cabeldue’s snaps a lot earlier than expected after he replaced Richman. Montorie Foster works extensively again, gets special teams reps this week After a goose egg on the special teams front last week, Seattle’s preseason star had five ST reps, which included hustling down the field as a gunner and teaming up with Emmanuel Henderson for a -1 yard punt return. Foster almost pulled in a diving grab for a touchdown in the first half, and caught his only pass on a Jalen Milroe pass to get out of a 2nd and 20 jam. Jake Bobo’s season is over, which means WR5 is a wide open spot. Foster may have the inside track with how he’s performed. Seattle Seahawks defensive snap counts Tyrice Knight and Patrick O’Connell get the night off Unless either one (or both) picked up a knock in practice, it’s very telling that neither Knight nor O’Connell suited up. You don’t normally have the second linebacker pairing deemed so valuable to the team that they get the night off. Knight’s roster spot was never in jeopardy, but O’Connell has seemingly etched a place on the 53. It was a busy night for Chazz Surratt and Chris Paul Jr as the third-string linebackers, with Aaron Smith and Power Echols also getting a good chunk of work. A.J. Finley’s roster chances seem strong Even independent of the Bud Clark injury , this is two weeks in a row in which Finley has been the starting safety. He played virtually the whole game, which was probably in part due to Rodney Thomas II also not being available. Finley has done well to recover from last year’s ACL tear, he’s had a good camp and preseason up to this point. Andre Fuller stays at nickel corner The Seahawks had Noah Igbinoghene and Nehemiah Pritchett as the boundary corners for the entirety of the first half. Someone had to play nickel, and that honor belonged to seventh-round rookie Andre Fuller. Actually, Fuller played into the second half and his position was unchanged even when alongside Michael Dansby and Jordan Washington. Without looking at every single snap, I think Fuller has been exclusively a slot guy, which is pretty interesting given his size (6’1 and about 200 lbs) seems more apt for the boundary. Two down, one to go. The Seahawks wrap up their preseason on Friday, Aug. 28 at the Kansas City Chiefs.

title: Seahawks injuries worst part of forgettable preseason loss at Titans
summary: For the second week in a row, the Seattle Seahawks lost a preseason game, fumbling (er…intercepting) their way to a 19-16 loss against the Tennessee Titans. The offense started off hot with Drew Lock leading another first drive TD once again helped by a penalty. Actually, the Seahawks scored on their first three drives and […]
full_text: Aug 23, 2026; Nashville, Tennessee, USA; Seattle Seahawks safety Bud Clark (9) is carted off against the Tennessee Titans during the first half at Nissan Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Steve Roberts-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect For the second week in a row, the Seattle Seahawks lost a preseason game, fumbling (er…intercepting) their way to a 19-16 loss against the Tennessee Titans . The offense started off hot with Drew Lock leading another first drive TD once again helped by a penalty. Actually, the Seahawks scored on their first three drives and took a 16-3 lead at halftime. The worst part of the first half were the injuries with Mason Richman going out during the first offensive drive and Bud Clark getting carted off the field on the first defensive snap. According to Mike Macdonald in his postgame presser, both Richman and Clark have long-term injuries . That’s in addition to Jake Bobo’s knee injury from the joint practice . Not good. The second half was a brutal watch once again filled with penalties, turnovers, and missed assignments. Seattle’s offense could stay on the field, and the defense bent repeatedly before finally breaking as the Titans scored the final 16 points of the game. It was a sloppy effort once again. Seahawks Droppings Jalen Milroe has seemingly lost all confidence . I’ve been firmly in Jalen Milroe’s corner since he was drafted, but even I must admit that he looks totally lost out there. Both of the interceptions he threw were awful for different reasons. On the first one, Milroe never saw the defender that was reading it the whole way. On the second, Milroe’s pass was behind the WR. Add to that the sack that he took on fourth down, and things are not looking pretty in Milroe land. Drew Lock looked like a competent backup QB once again . He was nearly perfect in the first half, though a questionable penalty called back an interception. Lock put his body on the line for a first down run, which the rest of the team will love. Jacardia Wright has some juice. I liked Wright last season and was bummed when he got injured. He’s got good size with enough burst to be dangerous as evidenced by his 69-yard TD scamper. Wright also showed that he can catch the ball, which will apparently be a huge part of the offense this season if tonight was anything to go by. Both Lock and Milroe were checking the ball down way more often than pushing it down the field. There was a little more pass rush tonight, notably from Connor O’Toole and Jamie Sheriff. Both of those guys are battling for a backup Edge roster spot. One more good week from either of them could secure their spot as one of the final 53. Should we start to be concerned about Jason Myers? He missed a kick in last week’s game and missed two more today. Myers has been incredibly consistent with the Seahawks, so there’s good history there…yet I’m not liking what I’m seeing so far in 2026. 25 combined penalties for 229 yards. And here, I thought last week was bad! I don’t know if the refs are just being flag-happy, but the constant laundry on the field makes the game hard to watch. Most of the flags were legit like the facemask on Jacardia Wright that turned his helmet completely around. Some of them shouldn’t have been called, and that goes for both the Titans and Seahawks. I guess the refs need work too. Seattle’s defense isn’t turning the ball over. You’d hope that during the preseason, the Seahawks defense could force some mistakes that end up as turnovers. Instead, it was the offense and special teams coughing the ball up leading to a -3 turnover differential. That makes it hard to win regardless of whether it’s preseason or not. The second half was disappointing for a number of reasons, but it’s really the Clark, Richman, and Bobo injuries that stick out from the Tennessee trip. None of the three were necessarily starters right now, yet each is core depth. Clark was competing for reps with the No. 1 defense. Richman was seemingly the third guard behind Grey Zabel and Anthony Bradford along with getting time at center. Bobo was a huge part of special teams and had a role as a backup receiver particularly known for his blocking. To lose all three for the season in a span of days is a gut punch. Mike Macdonald preaches a roster that’s 70 deep, and he along with John Schneider, will be tested to fill these gaps.
